7:17.arabic: قوله تعالى {وقليل من عبادي الشكور} وفرح إبليس لعنه الله بقوله {ولا تجد أكثرهم شاكرين} فلا يعرف معنى هذه الآية من لم يعرف معنى هذا كله وأمورا أخر وراء ذلك تنقضي الأعمار دون استقصاء مباديها فأما تفسير الآية ومعنى لفظها فيعرفه كل من يعرف اللغة وبهذا يتبين لك الفرق بين المعنى والتفسير فإن قلت فقد رجع حاصل هذا الكلام إلى أن الله تعالى حكمه في كل شيء وأنه جعل بعض أفعال العباد سببا لتمام الحكمة وبلوغها غاية المراد منها وجعل بعض أفعالها مانعا من تمام الحكمة فكل فعل وافق مقتضى الحكمة حتى انساقت الحكمة إلى غايتها فهو شكر وكل ما خالف ومن
7:17.english: ...from his hand, it could not be taken from him — not because the morsel became his property by the mere taking of the hand, for the hand and its owner are also owned [by God]. But rather, since every single morsel in its particularity does not suffice for the need of all the servants, justice in the specification (takhṣīṣ) [of provision] lies in the occurrence of a certain kind of preponderance and particularization; and the taking [by the hand] is a particularization (ikhtiṣāṣ) that the servant uniquely performs. Thus, whoever does not put forward that particularization is prevented from contesting him [who has taken it]. In this manner, you ought to understand the command of God — exalted — regarding His servants. And for this reason, we say: whoever takes from the wealth of this world more than his need, and hoards it and withholds it, while among the servants of God there are those who are in need of it — he is a wrongdoer (ẓālim), and he is among those who "hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God" {«يكنزون الذهب والفضة ولا ينفقونها في سبيل الله»}. And the "way of God" (sabīl Allāh) is only His obedience; and the means of creation to His obedience are the wealth of this world, for through it their necessities are repelled and their needs are lifted. Yes — this does not enter into the scope of the legal rulings (fatāwā) of jurisprudence, because the measures of needs are hidden, and souls differ in their anticipation of future poverty, and the ends of lifespans are unknown. Thus, charging the common folk with this would be like charging children with dignity, deliberateness, and silence from unimportant speech — which, by virtue of their deficiency, they cannot bear. So we have left off objecting to them regarding play and amusement, and our permitting that to them does not indicate that amusement and play are the truth. Likewise, our permitting the common folk to preserve wealth and to restrict spending to the amount of the alms-tax (zakāh), due to the necessity of the avarice they are naturally formed upon, does not indicate that this is the ultimate limit of truth. Indeed, the Qur'an has pointed to this when He — exalted — said: {«إن يسألكموها فيحفكم تبخلوا»} "If He asks you for them and presses you, you would be miserly." Rather, the truth that has no turbidity in it, and the justice that has no injustice in it, is that no one should take from the servants of God, from the wealth of God, except to the measure of the provision of a rider (zād al-rākib). For all the servants of God are riders upon the mounts of their bodies, journeying to the presence of the King, the Reckoner (al-Malik al-Dayyān). So whoever takes more than that, and then withholds it from another rider who is in need of it — he is a wrongdoer, abandoning justice, departing from the purpose of wisdom (ḥikmah), and ungrateful for the blessing of God — exalted — upon him, through the Qur'an, the Messenger, the intellect, and all the other means by which he came to know that whatever exceeds the rider's provision is a burden upon him in this world and the Hereafter. So whoever understands the wisdom of God — exalted — in all the kinds of existent things is able to undertake the duty of thankfulness (shukr). And exhausting that [understanding] requires volumes, and even then they would not suffice except for a little. And we have only mentioned this much so that the cause of the truthfulness in His saying — exalted: {«وقليل من عبادي الشكور»} "And few of My servants are thankful" — may be known, and the rejoicing of Iblis — may God curse him — in his saying: {«ولا تجد أكثرهم شاكرين»} "And you will not find most of them thankful." For no one knows the meaning of this verse who does not know the meaning of all of this, along with other matters beyond it, the lifetimes expiring without exhausting their principles. As for the interpretation (tafsīr) of the verse and the meaning of its wording, everyone who knows the language knows that. And by this, the difference between meaning (maʿnā) and interpretation (tafsīr) becomes clear to you. For if you say: "The sum of this discourse has returned to the claim that God — exalted — His judgment (ḥukm) is in everything, and that He made some acts of His servants a cause for the completion of wisdom and its reaching the ultimate purpose intended from it, and He made some of their acts a barrier to the completion of wisdom. So every act that conforms to the requirement of wisdom, such that wisdom flows on to its end, is thankfulness (shukr); and everything that opposes it and prevents the causes from flowing to the purpose intended by them is ungratefulness (kufrān). And all of this is understood. But the difficulty remains: the servant's act — divided into what completes wisdom and what lifts it — is itself also from the act of God — exalted. So where is the servant in between, such that he is thankful at one time and ungrateful at another?" — Know that the full realization of this draws its source from the current of a mighty sea of the sciences of unveiling (ʿulūm al-mukāshafāt). We have already alluded, in what preceded, to intimations of its principles. And now we shall express, with a concise utterance, its final end and ultimate goal — understood by whoever knows the logic of the birds (manṭiq al-ṭayr), and denied by whoever is incapable of quickening his pace in the journey, let alone soaring in the atmosphere of the Kingdom (malakūt) with the flight of birds. So we say: God — mighty and majestic — in His glory and supremacy, has an attribute from which creation and invention issue forth. And that attribute is higher and more exalted than that the eye of the language-coiner could perceive it, so as to express it with an utterance indicating the essence of its glory and the specificity of its reality. Thus, there is no expression for it in the world, due to the loftiness of its station and the lowness of the rank of the language-coiners from extending the reach of their understanding to the principles of its radiance. Their sights have fallen from its summit, just as the sights of bats fall from the light of the sun — not due to its obscurity...
7:17.section_title_en: The Reality of Shukr (Thankfulness) and the Distinction Between Meaning (Maʿnā) and Interpretation (Tafsīr)
7:17.anchors:
- Root: شكر (Sh-K-R)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes fullness (as in a brimming udder, ضرة شكرى) and the manifestation of increase; cognate with the notion of an animal thriving on little fodder.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الشكر: تصور النعمة وإظهارها" — Thankfulness is the conceptualization of the blessing and its outward manifestation. It is divided into three kinds: gratitude of the heart (perception of the blessing), of the tongue (praise of the Benefactor), and of the limbs (rewarding the blessing through obedience).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (Haqiqah): "شكرت لله تعالى نعمته" — verbal acknowledgment. Metaphorical (Majaz): "دابة شكور" — a beast that suffices on little fodder yet grows fat, symbolizing the one who fulfills the duty of gratitude with minimal worldly means.
- Root: ظلم (Ẓ-L-M)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Root denotes darkness (absence of light); placing something in other than its proper place.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Darkness is used metaphorically for ignorance, polytheism, and transgression, as opposed to light (nūr) which signifies knowledge and justice.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "الظلم ظلمات يوم القيامة" — injustice is darkness on the Day of Resurrection. Metaphorical: "أرض مظلومة" — land never before dug, i.e., one who hoards wealth without prior right or need.
- Root: حكم (H-K-M)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Root meaning: to prevent for the sake of correction; hence the reins (ḥikmah) of a horse.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "حكم أصله: منع منعا لإصلاح" — judgment/wise purpose is a restraining for rectification; God's ḥikmah is His ordering of creation toward its intended perfection.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "أحكم الشيء فاستحكم" — to make a thing firm and sound; God's wisdom is the firm ordering of all existents toward their ends.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction & Focused Predication) — Used to restrict the meaning of "سبيل الله" (the path of God) exclusively to obedience, and to delimit the true and unclouded justice as that of the traveler's provision (zād al-rākib).
7:17.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

7:137.arabic: وقال تعالى وتمت كلمة ربك الحسنى على بني إسرائيل بما صبروا وقال تعالى ولنجزين الذين صبروا أجرهم بأحسن ما كانوا يعملون وقال تعالى أولئك يؤتون أجرهم مرتين بما صبروا وقال تعالى إنما يوفى الصابرون أجرهم بغير حساب فما من قربة إلا وأجرها بتقدير وحساب إلا الصبر ولأجل كون الصوم من الصبر وأنه نصف الصبر قال الله تعالى الصوم لي وأنا أجزي به فأضافه إلى نفسه من بين سائر العبادات ووعد الصابرين بأنه معهم فقال تعالى واصبروا إن الله مع الصابرين وعلق النصرة على الصبر فقال تعالى بلى إن تصبروا وتتقوا ويأتوكم من فورهم هذا يم
7:137.english: Allah — exalted be He — has described the patient (al-ṣābirīn) with attributes, and He mentioned patience (al-ṣabr) in the Qur’an in upwards of seventy places. He attached most of the degrees and goods to patience, making them its fruit. For He said — majestic is His utterance: {«وَجَعَلْنَا مِنْهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا لَمَّا صَبَرُوا»} — “And We made from among them imams guiding by Our command, when they were patient” (Q 32:24). And He said — exalted be He: {«وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ الْحُسْنَىٰ عَلَىٰ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ بِمَا صَبَرُوا»} — “And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled upon the Children of Israel, because they were patient” (Q 7:137). And He said — exalted be He: {«وَلَنَجْزِيَنَّ الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا أَجْرَهُم بِأَحْسَنِ مَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ»} — “And We shall surely recompense those who were patient their wage according to the best of what they used to do” (Q 16:96). And He said — exalted be He: {«أُولَٰئِكَ يُؤْتَوْنَ أَجْرَهُم مَّرَّتَيْنِ بِمَا صَبَرُوا»} — “Those shall be given their wage twice, because they were patient” (Q 28:54). And He said — exalted be He: {«إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُم بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ»} — “Only the patient shall be paid their wage without reckoning” (Q 39:10). Thus there is no act of nearness (qurbah) whose wage is not meted out by measure and account — except patience. And because fasting (al-ṣawm) is of patience, and it is half of patience, Allah — exalted be He — said: “Fasting is Mine, and I recompense it” — so He attributed it to Himself, to the exclusion of all other acts of worship. And He promised the patient that He is with them, saying — exalted be He: {«وَاصْبِرُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ»} — “And be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient” (Q 8:46). And He made victory contingent upon patience, saying — exalted be He: {«بَلَىٰ إِن تَصْبِرُوا وَتَتَّقُوا وَيَأْتُوكُم مِّن فَوْرِهِمْ هَٰذَا يُمْدِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُم بِخَمْسَةِ آلَافٍ مِّنَ الْمَلَائِكَةِ مُسَوِّمِينَ»} — “Yes, if you are patient and God-fearing, and they come upon you in their rush, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand marked angels” (Q 3:125). And He gathered for the patient things He gathered for no others, saying — exalted be He: {«أُولَٰئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ وَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ»} — “Those — upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy; and those — they are the rightly guided” (Q 2:157). So guidance, mercy, and blessings are all gathered for the patient. And to exhaust all the verses concerning the station of patience would be lengthy.
7:137.section_title_en: The Virtue of Patience (Ṣabr) — Its Excellence in the Qur’an, Sunnah, and Reports of the Salaf
7:137.anchors:
- Root: صبر (Ṣ-B-R)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is “to restrain, to hold back, to bind firmly” — as in holding an animal by its halter or confining someone against departure.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Patience is “the self’s restraint upon what reason and Sacred Law require, or from what they require it to abstain from.” It is a generic term whose specific names vary by context: in calamity it is ṣabr (opposed to jazaʿ); in battle it is courage (shajāʿah); in vexation it is forbearance.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): “I bore patiently what I disliked, and I refrained patiently from what I loved.” Metaphorical (majāz): “His right hand was made to swear patiently” (i.e., bound by an emphatic oath), and “this tree is patient against cold” (i.e., unaffected by it).
- Root: عله (ʿ-L-H) — [Noted as a rare root; no direct bearing on this passage’s core terms, but included per lexical apparatus.]
- Root: ايم (A-Y-M) — [Noted as a rare root; no direct bearing on this passage’s core terms, but included per lexical apparatus.]
- Root: نفس (N-F-S)
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The self (nafs) as the locus of volitional restraint — patience is an act of the nafs holding itself back, distinguishing it from mere physical endurance.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: “a precious thing” (nafīs). Metaphorical: “he poured out his soul” (i.e., his blood), and “everything that has no flowing soul does not defile water.”
- Sibawayh Rule: Restriction and Focused Predication (Bāb al-Ḥaṣr wa al-Taqyīd bi-innamā) — Governing the exclusive clause {«إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُم بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ»}, where innamā restricts the reward-without-account solely to the patient, and {«الصَّوْمُ لِي وَأَنَا أَجْزِي بِهِ»}, where the predicate is focused to Allah alone.
7:137.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

7:194.arabic: {إن الذين تدعون من دون الله عباد أمثالكم} فالشكر باللسان من جملة الشكر وقد روي أن وفدا قدموا على عمر بن عبد العزيز رحمه الله فقام شاب ليتكلم فقال عمر الكبر الكبر فقال يا أمير المؤمنين لو كان الأمر بالسن لكان في المسلمين من هو أسكن منك فقال تكلم فقال لسنا وفد الرغبة ولا وفد الرهبة أما الرغبة فقد أوصلها إلينا فضلك وأما الرهبة فقد آمننا منها عدلك وإنما نحن وقد الشكر جئناك نشكرك باللسان وننصرف فهذه هي أصول معاني الشكر المحيطة بمجموع حقيقته فأما قول من قال إن الشكر هو الاعتراف بنعمة المنعم
7:194.english: ...not the vision of the blessing. And al-Khawwāṣ — God's mercy upon him — said: "The gratitude of the common folk is for food, clothing, and drink; the gratitude of the elite is for the arrivals upon the hearts [of divine gnosis]." This is a station that not everyone apprehends — those whose pleasures are confined to the belly, the loins, and the sensory perceptions of colors and sounds, and who are devoid of the heart's pleasure. For the heart, in a state of health, takes delight only in the remembrance of God — exalted is He — in knowledge of Him, and in the hope of meeting Him. It only delights in other than Him when it has fallen ill through evil habits — just as some people take pleasure in eating clay, and just as some of the sick find sweet things repugnant and bitter things sweet, as it was said:
7:194.section_title_en: The Reality of Gratitude (Shukr) — Its Three Pillars and the Degrees of the Thankful
7:194.anchors:
- Root: شكر (Sh-K-R)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is "to open, reveal, or fill"; a beast that thrives on little fodder is called *shakūr* — its fullness of body manifests its owner's care.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Gratitude is "the conceptualization of the blessing and its manifestation" (*taṣawwur al-niʿmah wa-iẓhāruhā*). It is the inverse of *kufr* (disbelief/ingratitude), which is forgetting and concealing the blessing. It has three kinds: gratitude of the heart (perceiving the blessing), of the tongue (praising the Benefactor), and of the limbs (requiting the blessing through obedience).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (*ḥaqīqah*): "I thanked God for His blessing." Metaphorical (*majāz*): A beast is called *shakūr* when little fodder suffices it and it fattens — the gratitude is manifest in its condition, not uttered by a tongue.
- Root: نعم (N-ʿ-M)
  * Lisan / Ayn: *Niʿmah* denotes a state of well-being and ease; *naʿīm* is the felicitous life therein.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): *Niʿmah* is "the good state" (*al-ḥālah al-ḥasanah*), built on the pattern of states like sitting (*jilsah*) and riding (*rikbah*). It applies to both little and much, as in {«وَإِن تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا»} (Ibrahim: 34).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "God's blessing and His bounties are immense." Metaphorical: "Their ostriches departed" (*khafat naʿāmatuhum*) — meaning they fled, a metaphor for the vanishing of comfort.
- Root: قلب (Q-L-B)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To turn a thing over, to rotate it from one face to another.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "The turning of a thing: directing it and moving it from one aspect to another." The heart is so named for its constant fluctuation (*taqallub*).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "I turned the thing over." Metaphorical: "A man *qalb ḥawal*" — one who turns matters over and devises stratagems; "they turned the matters over for you" (Quran 9:48), i.e., they examined and contrived.
- Sibawayh Rule: Restriction and Focused Predication (*al-ḥaṣr wa-al-taqyīd bi-innamā*) — The particle *innamā* restricts the predicate to the subject alone, as in the author's formulation "Gratitude is only the acknowledgment of the Benefactor's blessing in a posture of humility" — a definition that confines the reality to one part (the tongue with a state of the heart) rather than the whole.
7:194.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

8:28.arabic: وتعثر الحسن والنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم على منبره فنزل فحمله وقرأ قوله {إنما أموالكم وأولادكم فتنة} (3) وقال عبد الله بن شداد بينما رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يصلي بالناس إذ جاءه الحسين فركب عنقه وهو ساجد فأطال السجود بالناس حتى ظنوا أنه قد حدث أمر فلما قضى صلاته قالوا قد أطلت السجود يا رسول الله حتى ظننا أنه قد حدث أمر فقال إن ابني قد ارتحلني فكرهت أن أعجله حتى يقضي حاجته (4) وفي ذلك فوائد إحداها القرب من الله تعالى فإن العبد أقرب ما يكون من الله تعالى إذا كان ساجدا وفيه الرفق بالولد والبر وتعليم لأمته وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم ريح الو
8:28.english: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "A child will never repay his father until he finds him a slave, buys him, and sets him free."
8:28.section_title_en: The Book of the Revival of the Religious Sciences — Section 439: On the Rights of Parents and Children
8:28.anchors:
- Root: ولد (w-l-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To give birth, beget, produce; offspring, child, progeny.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-walad denotes the begotten, singular or plural, young or old; also used for an adopted child. The root signifies the direct causal link of generation.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical birth and kinship. Metaphorical (majāz) for "newly invented speech" (kalām muwallad) — but here, strictly literal.
- Root: بر (b-r-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Piety, dutifulness, kindness, gentleness; antonym of ʿuqūq (disobedience, severance).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Birr is expansive goodness that connects the servant to God and creation; its opposite is ʿuqūq, the cutting of what God has commanded to be joined.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal for filial piety and charitable excellence.
- Root: رحم (r-ḥ-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The womb; kinship, blood-tie; mercy, compassion.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Raḥim is the organ of gestation, and raḥmah is the mercy that God apportions; the kin-tie (raḥim) is so named because it demands mutual mercy.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal for the womb and blood-relations; metaphorical for mercy as its spiritual fruit.
- Sibawayh Rule: Rule of Restriction and Focused Predication (Bāb al-Ḥaṣr wa al-Taqyīd bi-innamā) — governing the exclusive force of statements like {«إنما أموالكم وأولادكم فتنة»}, where the predicate is restricted to the subject alone.
8:28.topic: Prophetic traditions and scholastic commentary by Al-Ghazali, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

8:44.arabic: القلوب قلة إلى أن تقرب الساعة ويقضي الله أمرا كان مفعولا وإنما وجب أن يكون هذا نادرا لأنه مبادي ملك الآخرة والملك عزيز والملوك لا يكثرون فكما لا يكون الفائق في الملك والجمال إلا نادرا وأكثر الناس من دونهم فكذا في ملك الآخرة فإن الدنيا مرآة الآخرة فإنها عبارة عن عالم الشهادة والآخرة عبارة عن عالم الغيب وعالم الشهادة تابع لعالم الغيب كما أن الصورة في المرآة تابعة لصورة الناظر في المرآة والصورة في المرآة وإن كانت هي الثانية في رتبة الوجود فإنها أولى في حق رؤيتك فإنك لا ترى نفسك وترى صورتك في المرآة أولا فتعرف
8:44.english: As for the first: if it is possible in existence at all, it is at the utmost extreme of remoteness. As for the second: the lower world is overflowing with it. As for the third and fourth: they exist, but at the utmost extreme of rarity. And it is inconceivable that this [rarity] should itself be rare and anomalous — rather, even with its rarity, it varies in degree of fewness and abundance. Its abundance occurs only in ages proximate to the ages of the Prophets, peace be upon them. The longer the interval [from their time] grows, the scarcer such hearts become, until the Hour draws near and God accomplishes a matter already decreed ( {وكان أمرا مفعولا} ).
8:44.section_title_en: The Division of Hearts and the Rarity of the Heart Fit for the Kingdom of the Hereafter
8:44.anchors:
- Root: م ل ك (Malaka)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of possession, dominion, and sovereign control; al-Ayn notes the pattern shift in derived nouns.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الملك: هو المتصرف بالأمر والنهي في الجمهور" — kingship is governance over rational beings, divided into actual sovereignty (al-tamalluk) and capacity for it (al-quwwah).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "لله الملك والملكوت" — dominion over the visible and invisible realms. Metaphorical: "ملك نفسه عند الغضب" — self-mastery; here extended to the heart's sovereignty over the soul's appetites.
- Root: ق ل ب (Qalaba)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Turning and overturning a thing from one state to another.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "قلب الشيء: تصريفه وصرفه عن وجه إلى وجه" — the heart is so named for its constant fluctuation between states.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "قلب الشيء قلبا: حوله عن وجهه." Metaphorical: "رجل قلب حول: يقلب الأمور ويحتال" — one who turns matters over; here, hearts are classified by their dominant orientation.
- Root: ع ل م (ʿAlima)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Foundational knowing and perception.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العلم: إدراك الشيء بحقيقته" — apprehension of a thing's true reality, of two kinds: grasping the essence, and judging its attributes.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "هو من أعلام العلم الخافقه" — knowledge as a raised banner. Here, "علم اليقين" (knowledge of certainty) vs. "عين اليقين" (eye of certainty) marks the literal-to-metaphorical ascent from inference to direct vision.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction & Focused Predication) — The repeated use of "إنما" (only/indeed) throughout this passage serves to restrict predicates exclusively to their subjects, e.g., "وإنما تكون كثرته في الأعصار القريبة" — restricting abundance to specific eras, and "وإنما وجب أن يكون هذا نادرا" — restricting the cause of rarity.
8:44.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

8:46.arabic: سائر العبادات ووعد الصابرين بأنه معهم فقال تعالى واصبروا إن الله مع الصابرين وعلق النصرة على الصبر فقال تعالى بلى إن تصبروا وتتقوا ويأتوكم من فورهم هذا يمددكم ربكم بخمسة آلاف من الملائكة مسومين وجمع للصابرين بين أمور لم يجمعها لغيرهم فقال تعالى أولئك عليهم صلوات من ربهم ورحمة وأولئك هم المهتدون فالهدى والرحمة والصلوات مجموعة للصابرين واستقصاء جميع الآيات في مقام الصبر يطول وأما الأخبار فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم الصبر نصف الإيمان (1) على ما سيأتي وجه كونه نصفا وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم من أقل ما أوتيتم اليقين وعزيمة الصبر ومن
8:46.english: Allah — exalted be He — has described the patient (al-ṣābirīn) with attributes, and He mentioned patience (al-ṣabr) in the Qur’an in upwards of seventy places. He attached most of the degrees and goods to patience, making them its fruit. For He said — majestic is His utterance: {«وَجَعَلْنَا مِنْهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا لَمَّا صَبَرُوا»} — “And We made from among them imams guiding by Our command, when they were patient” (Q 32:24). And He said — exalted be He: {«وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ الْحُسْنَىٰ عَلَىٰ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ بِمَا صَبَرُوا»} — “And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled upon the Children of Israel, because they were patient” (Q 7:137). And He said — exalted be He: {«وَلَنَجْزِيَنَّ الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا أَجْرَهُم بِأَحْسَنِ مَا كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ»} — “And We shall surely recompense those who were patient their wage according to the best of what they used to do” (Q 16:96). And He said — exalted be He: {«أُولَٰئِكَ يُؤْتَوْنَ أَجْرَهُم مَّرَّتَيْنِ بِمَا صَبَرُوا»} — “Those shall be given their wage twice, because they were patient” (Q 28:54). And He said — exalted be He: {«إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُم بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ»} — “Only the patient shall be paid their wage without reckoning” (Q 39:10). Thus there is no act of nearness (qurbah) whose wage is not meted out by measure and account — except patience. And because fasting (al-ṣawm) is of patience, and it is half of patience, Allah — exalted be He — said: “Fasting is Mine, and I recompense it” — so He attributed it to Himself, to the exclusion of all other acts of worship. And He promised the patient that He is with them, saying — exalted be He: {«وَاصْبِرُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ»} — “And be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient” (Q 8:46). And He made victory contingent upon patience, saying — exalted be He: {«بَلَىٰ إِن تَصْبِرُوا وَتَتَّقُوا وَيَأْتُوكُم مِّن فَوْرِهِمْ هَٰذَا يُمْدِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُم بِخَمْسَةِ آلَافٍ مِّنَ الْمَلَائِكَةِ مُسَوِّمِينَ»} — “Yes, if you are patient and God-fearing, and they come upon you in their rush, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand marked angels” (Q 3:125). And He gathered for the patient things He gathered for no others, saying — exalted be He: {«أُولَٰئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ وَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ»} — “Those — upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy; and those — they are the rightly guided” (Q 2:157). So guidance, mercy, and blessings are all gathered for the patient. And to exhaust all the verses concerning the station of patience would be lengthy.
8:46.section_title_en: The Virtue of Patience (Ṣabr) — Its Excellence in the Qur’an, Sunnah, and Reports of the Salaf
8:46.anchors:
- Root: صبر (Ṣ-B-R)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is “to restrain, to hold back, to bind firmly” — as in holding an animal by its halter or confining someone against departure.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Patience is “the self’s restraint upon what reason and Sacred Law require, or from what they require it to abstain from.” It is a generic term whose specific names vary by context: in calamity it is ṣabr (opposed to jazaʿ); in battle it is courage (shajāʿah); in vexation it is forbearance.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): “I bore patiently what I disliked, and I refrained patiently from what I loved.” Metaphorical (majāz): “His right hand was made to swear patiently” (i.e., bound by an emphatic oath), and “this tree is patient against cold” (i.e., unaffected by it).
- Root: عله (ʿ-L-H) — [Noted as a rare root; no direct bearing on this passage’s core terms, but included per lexical apparatus.]
- Root: ايم (A-Y-M) — [Noted as a rare root; no direct bearing on this passage’s core terms, but included per lexical apparatus.]
- Root: نفس (N-F-S)
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The self (nafs) as the locus of volitional restraint — patience is an act of the nafs holding itself back, distinguishing it from mere physical endurance.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: “a precious thing” (nafīs). Metaphorical: “he poured out his soul” (i.e., his blood), and “everything that has no flowing soul does not defile water.”
- Sibawayh Rule: Restriction and Focused Predication (Bāb al-Ḥaṣr wa al-Taqyīd bi-innamā) — Governing the exclusive clause {«إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى الصَّابِرُونَ أَجْرَهُم بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ»}, where innamā restricts the reward-without-account solely to the patient, and {«الصَّوْمُ لِي وَأَنَا أَجْزِي بِهِ»}, where the predicate is focused to Allah alone.
8:46.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

8:63.arabic: قال الله تعالى مظهرا عظيم منته على الخلق بنعمة الألفة {لو أنفقت ما في الأرض جميعا ما ألفت بين قلوبهم ولكن الله ألف بينهم} وقال {فأصبحتم بنعمته إخوانا} أي بالألفة ثم ذم التفرقة وزجر عنها فقال عز من قائل واعتصموا بحبل الله جميعا ولا تفرقوا إلى لعلكم تهتدون وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم إن أقربكم مني مجلسا أحاسنكم أخلاقا الموطئون أكنافا الذين يألفون ويؤلفون (2) وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم المؤمن آلف مألوف ولا خير فيمن لا يألف ولا يؤلف حديث والمؤمن آلف مألوف ولا خير فيمن لا يألف ولا يؤلف رواه أحمد والطبراني من حديث سهل بن سعد والحاكم من حديث أبي هريرة وصححه (3) حديث من أرا
8:63.english: Know that affability (al-ulfah) is the fruit of excellent character (ḥusn al-khuluq), and estrangement (al-tafarruq) is the fruit of evil character. For excellent character necessitates mutual love, harmony, and concord, whereas evil character yields mutual hatred, envy, and turning away (al-tadābur). And whenever the source is praiseworthy, the fruit is likewise praiseworthy. The excellence of good character is not hidden in the religion; indeed, it is that with which God—glorified be He—praised His Prophet, peace be upon him, when He said: {وَإِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ} «And indeed, you are upon an immense character» (Al-Qalam: 4). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The thing which most causes people to enter Paradise is God-consciousness (taqwā) and excellent character." (1) Usāmah ibn Sharīk said: "We said, O Messenger of God, what is the best thing given to a person?" He said: "Excellent character." (2) He, peace be upon him, also said: "I was sent only to perfect the noble traits of character." (3) He, peace be upon him, said: "Nothing is heavier in the Balance than excellent character." (4) He, peace be upon him, said: "God does not beautify a person's outward form and his inward character, then feed him to the Fire." (5) He, peace be upon him, said: "O Abū Hurayrah, adhere to excellent character." (Page V02P157) Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, said: "What is excellent character, O Messenger of God?" He said: "That you join the one who cuts you off, forgive the one who wrongs you, and give to the one who deprives you." (1)
8:63.section_title_en: The Book of the Revival of the Religious Sciences — Section 402: On the Excellence of Affability (Al-Ulfah) and Brotherhood in God
8:63.anchors:
- Root: ألف (Alifa)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of harmonizing, uniting, and reconciling; the removal of estrangement (al-waḥshah) and the establishment of concord.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological nuance of ta'līf as the divine act of harmonizing hearts, a blessing bestowed by God alone, as in {لَوْ أَنفَقْتَ مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًا مَّا أَلَّفْتَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِهِمْ}.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) denotes physical joining; metaphorical (majāz) denotes the spiritual and moral concord of hearts, which is the fruit of excellent character (ḥusn al-khuluq).
- Root: خلق (Khalaqa)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Root meaning of measuring, proportioning, and smoothing; hence, the inherent disposition and moral character of a person.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The origination of a thing upon a just measure; for character, it is the inward form (al-ṣūrah al-bāṭinah) of the soul, just as the physical form is its outward shape.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is the physical creation and proportioning; metaphorical (majāz) is the moral and spiritual constitution, praised by God in {وَإِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ}.
- Root: بغض (Bughḍ)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The opposite of love (ḥubb); intense aversion and hatred.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): In the Kalam context, al-bughḍ fī Allāh (hatred for God's sake) is a spiritual act of discernment and loyalty, not a mere emotional impulse; it is paired with al-ḥubb fī Allāh as the strongest bond of faith (awthaq ʿurā al-īmān).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is personal animosity; metaphorical (majāz) is the righteous aversion to disobedience and the enemies of God, which is a form of devotion.
- Sibawayh Rule: Rule of Prepositional Interposition (Bāb al-Faṣl bayna al-Jār wa al-Majrūr) — Governing the syntactic flow of conditional and relative clauses, ensuring the periodic structure of the author's argument remains coherent and unbroken.
8:63.topic: Prophetic traditions and scholastic commentary by Al-Ghazali, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

8:63.arabic: مبتدع وليس بمتبع فلن يبلغ أحد مد أحدهم ولا نصيفه ولو انفق ما في الأرض جميعا كيف وقد أكل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم طعام بريرة فقيل: إنه صدقة فقال:
8:63.english: They said: "It is scrupulousness (al-waraʿ)." But Ḥassān ibn Abī Sinān said to them: "Nothing is easier for me than scrupulousness — whenever anything stirs unease in my breast, I simply leave it."
8:63.section_title_en: The Ruling on the Unknown Provider — Between Scrupulousness (Waraʿ) and Suspicion
8:63.anchors:
- Root: ورع (w-r-ʿ)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of restraint, abstaining, and holding back from what is doubtful or forbidden.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Waraʿ is the virtue of the God-fearing — abstaining not only from the unlawful but from the ambiguous (shubhah), as a safeguard for religion.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage denotes physical withdrawal; metaphorical usage denotes moral abstention — the heart's recoil from what is suspect.
- Root: ظن (ẓ-n-n)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Uncertainty, conjecture, or opinion that falls short of certainty.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Ẓann is divided into blameworthy suspicion (sūʾ al-ẓann) against the innocent — which is prohibited — and praiseworthy presumption of good (ḥusn al-ẓann) toward a Muslim, which is obligated by brotherhood in faith.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: to hold an opinion. Metaphorical: the heart's inclination toward one of two possibilities without decisive evidence.
- Root: ريبة (r-y-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Doubt, unease, or suspicion arising from a tangible indicator — not mere whim.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Rayb is the disturbance of certainty by an ambiguous circumstance; it is the legitimate trigger for inquiry, unlike baseless suspicion.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: uncertainty. Metaphorical: the inward disquiet that prompts a man to investigate before acting.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد (Restriction & Focused Predication) — The conditional and exceptive structures here (e.g., "لا يلزمك السؤال" and "إلا عن ريبة") restrict the obligation of inquiry to the presence of a genuine ground for doubt, not to mere possibility.
8:63.topic: Classical commentary from Al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din, from 'The Lawful and Prohibited'

9:15.arabic: ويغفر ما دون ذلك لمن يشاء {وقال} ويتوب الله على من يشاء وهو خلق من أخلاق الربوبية إذ قال تعالى والله شكور حليم وقد جعل الله الشكر مفتاح كلام أهل الجنة فقال تعالى وقالوا الحمد لله الذي صدقناه وعده {وقال} وآخر دعواهم أن الحمد لله رب العالمين
9:15.english: So then, what we have mentioned concerning the treatment of patience (ṣabr) regarding whispered insinuation (waswās), regarding lust (shahwah), and regarding status (jāh) — annex this to what we have already set down concerning the canons of the paths of spiritual striving (mujāhadah) in the Book of the Discipline of the Soul (Kitāb Riyāḍat al-Nafs) from the Quarter of the Destroyers (rubʿ al-muhlikāt). Adopt it as your manual (dastūr) by which you may come to know the treatment of patience in all the categories which we have previously detailed; for the detailing of individual cases is prolix. Whoever observes gradual progression (tadrīj), patience will elevate him to a state wherein patience without it becomes as arduous as it once was with it — so his affairs become inverted, and what was once beloved to him becomes loathed, and what was once detested to him becomes a sweet, wholesome draught from which he cannot bear to be patient [in abstaining]. This is known only through experience (tajribah) and tasting (dhawq). It has an analogue in customary habits: for a boy is compelled to learning in the beginning by force, and so patience with play and patience with knowledge are both arduous for him — until, when his inner sight is opened and he finds intimacy with knowledge, the matter is inverted, and it becomes arduous for him to be patient in abstaining from knowledge, and to endure play. To this points what is narrated of one of the knowers (ʿārifīn) that he asked al-Shiblī: "Patience — which of its kinds is the most severe?" He said: "Patience in God (fī Allāh)." He said: "No." He said: "Patience for God (li-Allāh)." He said: "No." He said: "Patience with God (maʿa Allāh)." He said: "No." He said: "Then what?" He said: "Patience from God (ʿan Allāh)." At that al-Shiblī cried out a cry by which his soul nearly perished. And it has been said concerning the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: {«اصبروا وصابروا ورابطوا»} "Be patient, and vie in patience, and be steadfast" (Q. 3:200): "Be patient in God, vie in patience by God, and be steadfast with God." And it was said: "Patience for God is sufficiency (ghināʾ); patience by God is endurance (baqāʾ); patience with God is fidelity (wafāʾ); and patience from God is abandonment (jafāʾ)." And it was said concerning its meaning:
9:15.section_title_en: The Revival of the Religious Sciences — Section 972: On Patience (al-Sabr) and the Commencement of Gratitude (al-Shukr)
9:15.anchors:
- Root: صبر (ṣ-b-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of restraint and withholding; al-Khalil notes its application to holding back an animal from fodder, and to enduring constraint.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الصبر: الإمساك في ضيق" — the withholding of the self in constriction; it is a general term whose specific names (shajāʿah, ḥilm, etc.) vary by context, and its opposite is al-jazaʿ (panic/vexation).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "صبرت على ما أكره. وصبرت عما أحب" — enduring what is disliked and restraining from what is loved. Metaphorical (majāz): "صبرت يمينه" — binding an oath strenuously; "أصبر على الضرب من الأرض" — more enduring than the earth.
- Root: شكر (sh-k-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The root denotes manifestation and fullness; al-Ayn links it to an overflowing udder (shukrā).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الشكر: تصور النعمة وإظهارها" — the perception of a blessing and its display; it is the opposite of kufr (covering/denial). It has three degrees: of the heart (perception), of the tongue (praise), and of the limbs (requital).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "شكرت لله تعالى نعمته" — thanking God for His grace. Metaphorical: "دابة شكور" — a beast that thrives on little fodder, displaying its owner's care through its fatness.
- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Knowledge as the apprehension of a thing's reality; al-Ayn treats it under the entry of umm (source/origin), indicating that knowledge is the root to which all else is annexed.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العلم: إدراك الشيء بحقيقته" — apprehension of a thing by its true reality, either by grasping its essence or by affirming/denying a predicate of it.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "ما علمت بخبرك: ما شعرت به" — to be aware/perceive. It is also used for the landmarks (maʿālim) of the road, i.e., traces by which one is guided.
- Root: وقد (w-q-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The kindling and blazing of fire; al-Ayn records it under the entry of w-q-d with the sense of fuel and flame.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "وقدت النار تقد وقودا ووقدا" — the fire blazed; al-wuqūd is both the fuel and the resulting flame, as in {«وقودها الناس والحجارة»} (Q. 2:24).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "وقدت النار وقودا ووقدا، واتقدت وتوقدت" — the fire blazed and blazed fiercely. Metaphorical: "قلب وقاد" — a blazing, keen heart; "وقدة الصيف" — the blazing heat of summer.
- Sibawayh Rule: Interposition between the operative word and its object (al-faṣl bayna al-ʿāmil wa al-maʿmūl fīhi) — governing the placement of circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) and prepositional phrases to preserve the intended semantic restriction, as in the verse "اصبروا وصابروا ورابطوا" where each imperative carries a distinct operative scope.

  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of restraint and withholding; al-Khalil notes its application to holding back an animal from fodder, and to enduring constraint.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الصبر: الإمساك في ضيق" — the withholding of the self in constriction; it is a general term whose specific names (shajāʿah, ḥilm, etc.) vary by context, and its opposite is al-jazaʿ (panic/vexation).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "صبرت على ما أكره. وصبرت عما أحب" — enduring what is disliked and restraining from what is loved. Metaphorical (majāz): "صبرت يمينه" — binding an oath strenuously; "أصبر على الضرب من الأرض" — more enduring than the earth.
- Root: شكر (sh-k-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The root denotes manifestation and fullness; al-Ayn links it to an overflowing udder (shukrā).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الشكر: تصور النعمة وإظهارها" — the perception of a blessing and its display; it is the opposite of kufr (covering/denial). It has three degrees: of the heart (perception), of the tongue (praise), and of the limbs (requital).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "شكرت لله تعالى نعمته" — thanking God for His grace. Metaphorical: "دابة شكور" — a beast that thrives on little fodder, displaying its owner's care through its fatness.
- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Knowledge as the apprehension of a thing's reality; al-Ayn treats it under the entry of umm (source/origin), indicating that knowledge is the root to which all else is annexed.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العلم: إدراك الشيء بحقيقته" — apprehension of a thing by its true reality, either by grasping its essence or by affirming/denying a predicate of it.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "ما علمت بخبرك: ما شعرت به" — to be aware/perceive. It is also used for the landmarks (maʿālim) of the road, i.e., traces by which one is guided.
- Root: وقد (w-q-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The kindling and blazing of fire; al-Ayn records it under the entry of w-q-d with the sense of fuel and flame.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "وقدت النار تقد وقودا ووقدا" — the fire blazed; al-wuqūd is both the fuel and the resulting flame, as in {«وقودها الناس والحجارة»} (Q. 2:24).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "وقدت النار وقودا ووقدا، واتقدت وتوقدت" — the fire blazed and blazed fiercely. Metaphorical: "قلب وقاد" — a blazing, keen heart; "وقدة الصيف" — the blazing heat of summer.
- Sibawayh Rule: Interposition between the operative word and its object (al-faṣl bayna al-ʿāmil wa al-maʿmūl fīhi) — governing the placement of circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) and prepositional phrases to preserve the intended semantic restriction, as in the verse "اصبروا وصابروا ورابطوا" where each imperative carries a distinct operative scope.
9:28.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

9:28.arabic: وقد قال الله تعالى يا أيها الذين آمنوا أنفقوا من طيبات ما كسبتم ومما أخرجنا لكم من الأرض ولا تيمموا الخبيث منه تنفقون ولستم بآخذيه إلا أن تغمضوا فيه أي لا تأخذوه إلا مع كراهية وحياء وهو معنى الإغماض فلا تؤثروا به ربكم وفي الخبر سبق درهم مائة ألف درهم (3) وذلك بأن يخرجه الإنسان وهو من أحل ماله وأجوده فيصدر ذلك عن الرضا والفرح بالبذل وقد يخرج مائة ألف درهم مما يكره من ماله فيدل ذلك على أنه ليس يؤثر الله عز وجل بشيء مما يحبه وبذلك ذم الله تعالى قوما جعلوا لله ما يكرهون فقال تعال
9:28.english: The heart is not treated save with the compound electuary (maʿjūn) of knowledge and works. And this condition among the conditions of almsgiving runs in the same course as humility (al-khushūʿ) runs in the prayer. This is established by his saying — may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "A man has nothing of his prayer save that of which he was conscious." And this is like his saying — may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Allah does not accept the charity of the one who bestows it with reproach (al-mannān)." And like His saying — Exalted is He: {«لا تبطلوا صدقاتكم بالمن والأذى»} ("Do not nullify your charities by reproach and injury"). As for the legal opinion (fatwā) of the jurist that the alms fall in their proper place and that one's liability is discharged without this condition — that is another discussion, and we have already pointed to its meaning in the Book of Prayer.
9:28.section_title_en: The Inner Conditions of Charity — Section 175 (From The Revival of the Religious Sciences, Book of the Mysteries of Almsgiving)
9:28.anchors:
- Root: قلب (q-l-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: "To turn, overturn, transform a thing from one state to another; to rotate, to flip"
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "قلب الشيء: تصريفه وصرفه عن وجه إلى وجه" — the heart is so named because of its constant turning and transformation between states
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "قلب الشيء قلبا: حوله عن وجهه" (to turn a thing from its face). Metaphorical: "رجل قلب حول: يقلب الأمور ويحتال" — one who turns matters over and manages them; "قلبوا لك الأمور" (they turned matters against you)
- Root: وجل (w-j-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: "Fear, dread, apprehension that strikes the heart"
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الوجل: استشعار الخوف" — the sensing of fear; cited in {«إنما المؤمنون الذين إذا ذكر الله وجلت قلوبهم»}
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "رجل وجل، وقوم وجال" — a fearful man, a fearful people; "وفي قلبه وجل" — in his heart is dread
- Root: عجب (ʿ-j-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: "Wonder, amazement; self-admiration, vanity"
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Self-admiration (al-ʿujb) is a destructive spiritual ailment that nullifies deeds
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: wonder at something extraordinary. Metaphorical: self-conceit regarding one's own acts of obedience
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد (Restriction & Focused Predication) — governing the precise limitation of general categories (al-ṣifāt al-khāṣṣah within al-aṣnāf al-thamāniyyah) and the conditional structure of acceptance

9:38.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Duties of Brotherhood'

9:38.arabic: أصلا فنادوا فيهم يا أيها الذين آمنوا ما لكم إذا قيل لكم انفروا في سبيل الله اثاقلتم إلى الأرض أرضيتم بالحياة الدنيا من الآخرة فما متاع الحياة الدنيا في الآخرة إلا قليل فالتوراة والإنجيل والزبور والفرقان وصحف موسى وإبراهيم وكل كتاب منزل ما أنزل إلالدعوة الخلق إلى الملك الدائم المخلد والمراد منهم أن يكونوا ملوكا في الدنيا ملوكا في الآخرة أما ملك الدنيا فالزهد فيها والقناعة باليسير منها وأما ملك الآخرة فبالقرب من الله تعالى يدرك بقاء لا فناء فيه وعزا لا ذل فيه وقرة عين أخفيت في هذا العالم لا تعلمها نفس من النفوس والشيطان يدعوهم إلى ملك الدنيا لعلمه بأن ملك الآخرة يفوت به إذ الدنيا والآخرة ضرتان ولعلمه بأن الدنيا لا تس
9:38.english: Al-Junayd — may Allah have mercy on him — said: "The journey from this world to the Hereafter is easy for the believer, but abandoning creation out of love for the Truth is severe. The journey from the self to Allah — exalted is He — is difficult and severe, and patience *with* Allah is even more severe." So he mentioned the severity of patience regarding the distractions of the heart, then the severity of abandoning creation.
9:38.section_title_en: The Cure for Patience Regarding Whispers and Distractions — The Final Station of Patience
9:38.anchors:
- Root: ملك (malaka)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of possession, dominion, and sovereign authority; al-mulk is that which is grasped and held under one's control.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-Mulk is of two kinds: (1) possession and assumption of authority (al-tamalluk wa al-tawallī), and (2) the inherent capacity/power for it (al-quwwah ʿalā dhālika), whether or not one actually assumes it. True sovereignty belongs to Allah alone; human "kingship" is a shadow or metaphor of divine rubūbiyyah.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "Li-llāh al-mulk wa al-malakūt" — dominion is real for God. Metaphorical (majāz): "malaka nafsahu ʿinda al-ghaḍab" (he mastered himself in anger) — self-possession as figurative rule; "malaka ʿalayhi amruhu" (his affair overcame him) — being dominated by external circumstance.
- Root: دنا (danā)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Proximity, nearness; al-dunyā (the lower/ nearer world) is so named because it is nearer to us and temporally prior, while the ākhirah is deferred.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-dunūw is nearness by essence or by judgment, used of place, time, and station. The "nearer" (al-adnā) is sometimes contrasted with the greater, sometimes with the better — as in {«أَتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ الَّذِي هُوَ أَدْنَى بِالَّذِي هُوَ خَيْرٌ»} (Do you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: physical proximity. Metaphorical: preference for the immediate over the deferred — the dunyā as the "present" that seduces the impatient.
- Root: خلق (khalaqa)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Originary measuring and fashioning; estimation before cutting; creation as bringing into being upon a determined measure.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-khalq is origination from no prior model (ibdāʿ), as in {«خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ»} — He originated them. Also used for bringing forth from something, as man from a drop. The "command" (amr) belongs to a different order than the "creation" (khalq).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: the tailor's measuring of cloth before cutting. Metaphorical: Allah's creation of beings upon a measure necessitated by wisdom; "khalq" as the fashioned body vs. "amr" as the commanding, immaterial reality.
- Root: الي (aliha / risālah)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The root of mal'akah (messengership) — that which is "chewed" in the mouth, i.e., conveyed by utterance; the angel as one who delivers a message.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-malā'ikah (angels) are so named from al-mal'akah (the message), because they deliver what is "masticated" in speech — from "faras ya'luku al-lijām" (a horse chewing the bit). The spirit (al-rūḥ) is from the "command" (amr) of the Lord — a subtle, immaterial reality.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: physical chewing. Metaphorical: the conveyance of divine communication through angelic intermediaries.
- Sibawayh Rule: Bāb al-ḥaṣr wa al-taqyīd bi-innamā (Restriction and Focused Predication) — "Innamā" restricts the predicate exclusively to the subject, as in {«إِنَّمَا مَتَاعُ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا فِي الْآخِرَةِ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ»} — the restriction here nullifies any comparison between the two realms, affirming the utter insignificance of worldly goods against the Hereafter.
9:38.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

9:96.arabic: وبين أن يستعملها في معصيته فقد كفر لاقتحامه ما يكرهه مولاه ولا يرضاه له فإن الله لا يرضى لعباده الكفر والمعصية وإن عطلها ولم يستعملها في طاعة ولا معصية فهو أيضا كفر كفران إن للنعمة بالتضييع وكل ما خلق في الدنيا إنما خلق آلة للعبد ليتوصل به إلى سعادة الآخرة ونيل القرب من الله تعالى فكل مطيع فهو بقدر طاعته شاكر نعمة الله في الأسباب التي استعملها في الطاعة وكل كسلان ترك الاستعمال أو عاص استعملها في طريق البعد فهو كافر جار في غير محبة الله تعالى فالمعصية والطاعة تشملهما المشيئة ولكن لا تشملهما المحبة والكراهة بل رب مراد
9:96.english: The hadith has already been presented in the Book of Repentance, and before that in the Book of Supplications. That was because of his ascent to seventy stations, some of which are above others. Its beginning — even though it surpassed the utmost limits of [all] creatures — was nevertheless a deficiency relative to its end. Thus his seeking forgiveness was for that [deficiency]. And when ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "Has God not forgiven you what preceded of your sin and what came after? Then what is this weeping in prostration, and what is this severe exertion?" — PageV04P087 — he {said}: "Shall I not then be a grateful servant?" // The hadith of ʿĀʾishah, when she said to him: "God has forgiven you what preceded of your sin and what came after — so what is this weeping?" — the hadith was narrated by Abū al-Shaykh, and it is the remainder of the hadith of ʿAṭāʾ from her, which preceded this by nine hadiths. It is also in Muslim from the narration of ʿUrwah from her, in abbreviated form. Likewise it is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, abbreviated, from the hadith of al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah. Its meaning is: "Shall I not be a seeker of increase in the stations?" — for gratitude is the cause of increase, as God Most High said: {«لئن شكرتم لأزيدنكم»} ["If you are grateful, I will surely increase you"].
9:96.section_title_en: The Reality of Gratitude and Ingratitude — The Parable of the King and the Servant
9:96.anchors:
- Root: شكر (sh-k-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of "opening/disclosing" (kashf) — the opposite of kufr, which is "covering/concealing"; also linked to a full udder (shukrā), i.e., abundance and fullness.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Gratitude is "the conceptualization of the blessing and its manifestation" — threefold: gratitude of the heart (perceiving the blessing), of the tongue (praising the Bestower), and of the limbs (rewarding the blessing through obedience).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (haqīqah): "I thanked God for His blessing." Metaphorical (majāz): A beast that suffices on little fodder yet fattens — gratitude as efficient use of provision for its intended purpose.
- Root: عبد (ʿ-b-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Servitude as manifest humility; ʿibādah is the utmost degree of self-abasement before the One deserving ultimate beneficence.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): ʿUbūdiyyah is "displaying humility," while ʿibādah is its extreme — and is of two kinds: by compulsion (all creatures) and by choice (the rational, who are commanded to worship).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "He is a servant (ʿabd) between servitude." Metaphorical: "So-and-so has enslaved me (taʿabbadanī)" — making one like a servant.
- Root: خلق (kh-l-q)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Originary estimation and measuring out (taqdīr) — creation as precise ordainment.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "Creation is originally: precise estimation (al-taqdīr al-mustaqīm)" — used for bringing forth from nothing (ibdāʿ) and for fashioning from existing matter.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: The leatherworker "estimates" (khalq) the hide before cutting. Metaphorical: "God created the creation" — brought them into being upon an estimation necessitated by wisdom.
- Root: قرب (q-r-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Nearness in place or station; the opposite of buʿd (distance).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Nearness to God is not spatial but by rank, honor, and obedience — the soul's proximity to the divine presence through virtuous acts.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: physical proximity. Metaphorical: "nearness to the King" — honor and favor, not spatial contiguity.
- Sibawayh Rule: Restriction and Focused Predication (al-ḥaṣr wa al-taqyīd bi-innamā) — "إنما الشرع كله تعريف طريق" restricts the entire purpose of the Sacred Law to one function: defining the path. Also, conditional and bipartite clauses (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) governing "مهما لبس العبد الثوب... فقد شكر" — the protasis-apodosis structure establishing a causal equivalence between action and its moral verdict.
9:96.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

10:10.arabic: الجنة فقال تعالى وقالوا الحمد لله الذي صدقناه وعده {وقال} وآخر دعواهم أن الحمد لله رب العالمين
10:10.english: So then, what we have mentioned concerning the treatment of patience (ṣabr) regarding whispered insinuation (waswās), regarding lust (shahwah), and regarding status (jāh) — annex this to what we have already set down concerning the canons of the paths of spiritual striving (mujāhadah) in the Book of the Discipline of the Soul (Kitāb Riyāḍat al-Nafs) from the Quarter of the Destroyers (rubʿ al-muhlikāt). Adopt it as your manual (dastūr) by which you may come to know the treatment of patience in all the categories which we have previously detailed; for the detailing of individual cases is prolix. Whoever observes gradual progression (tadrīj), patience will elevate him to a state wherein patience without it becomes as arduous as it once was with it — so his affairs become inverted, and what was once beloved to him becomes loathed, and what was once detested to him becomes a sweet, wholesome draught from which he cannot bear to be patient [in abstaining]. This is known only through experience (tajribah) and tasting (dhawq). It has an analogue in customary habits: for a boy is compelled to learning in the beginning by force, and so patience with play and patience with knowledge are both arduous for him — until, when his inner sight is opened and he finds intimacy with knowledge, the matter is inverted, and it becomes arduous for him to be patient in abstaining from knowledge, and to endure play. To this points what is narrated of one of the knowers (ʿārifīn) that he asked al-Shiblī: "Patience — which of its kinds is the most severe?" He said: "Patience in God (fī Allāh)." He said: "No." He said: "Patience for God (li-Allāh)." He said: "No." He said: "Patience with God (maʿa Allāh)." He said: "No." He said: "Then what?" He said: "Patience from God (ʿan Allāh)." At that al-Shiblī cried out a cry by which his soul nearly perished. And it has been said concerning the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: {«اصبروا وصابروا ورابطوا»} "Be patient, and vie in patience, and be steadfast" (Q. 3:200): "Be patient in God, vie in patience by God, and be steadfast with God." And it was said: "Patience for God is sufficiency (ghināʾ); patience by God is endurance (baqāʾ); patience with God is fidelity (wafāʾ); and patience from God is abandonment (jafāʾ)." And it was said concerning its meaning:
10:10.section_title_en: The Revival of the Religious Sciences — Section 972: On Patience (al-Sabr) and the Commencement of Gratitude (al-Shukr)
10:10.anchors:
- Root: صبر (ṣ-b-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of restraint and withholding; al-Khalil notes its application to holding back an animal from fodder, and to enduring constraint.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الصبر: الإمساك في ضيق" — the withholding of the self in constriction; it is a general term whose specific names (shajāʿah, ḥilm, etc.) vary by context, and its opposite is al-jazaʿ (panic/vexation).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "صبرت على ما أكره. وصبرت عما أحب" — enduring what is disliked and restraining from what is loved. Metaphorical (majāz): "صبرت يمينه" — binding an oath strenuously; "أصبر على الضرب من الأرض" — more enduring than the earth.
- Root: شكر (sh-k-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The root denotes manifestation and fullness; al-Ayn links it to an overflowing udder (shukrā).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الشكر: تصور النعمة وإظهارها" — the perception of a blessing and its display; it is the opposite of kufr (covering/denial). It has three degrees: of the heart (perception), of the tongue (praise), and of the limbs (requital).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "شكرت لله تعالى نعمته" — thanking God for His grace. Metaphorical: "دابة شكور" — a beast that thrives on little fodder, displaying its owner's care through its fatness.
- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Knowledge as the apprehension of a thing's reality; al-Ayn treats it under the entry of umm (source/origin), indicating that knowledge is the root to which all else is annexed.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العلم: إدراك الشيء بحقيقته" — apprehension of a thing by its true reality, either by grasping its essence or by affirming/denying a predicate of it.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "ما علمت بخبرك: ما شعرت به" — to be aware/perceive. It is also used for the landmarks (maʿālim) of the road, i.e., traces by which one is guided.
- Root: وقد (w-q-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The kindling and blazing of fire; al-Ayn records it under the entry of w-q-d with the sense of fuel and flame.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "وقدت النار تقد وقودا ووقدا" — the fire blazed; al-wuqūd is both the fuel and the resulting flame, as in {«وقودها الناس والحجارة»} (Q. 2:24).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "وقدت النار وقودا ووقدا، واتقدت وتوقدت" — the fire blazed and blazed fiercely. Metaphorical: "قلب وقاد" — a blazing, keen heart; "وقدة الصيف" — the blazing heat of summer.
- Sibawayh Rule: Interposition between the operative word and its object (al-faṣl bayna al-ʿāmil wa al-maʿmūl fīhi) — governing the placement of circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) and prepositional phrases to preserve the intended semantic restriction, as in the verse "اصبروا وصابروا ورابطوا" where each imperative carries a distinct operative scope.
10:10.topic: Al-Ghazali on supplications, prayers, and their spiritual power, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

10:24.arabic: في أكفانهم تحت الصعيد إن ملكت واحدا منهم جميع ما طلعت عليه الشمس جعلته حصيدا كأن لم يغن بالأمس تمنى أصحابها سرورا وتعدهم غرورا حتى يأملون كثيرا ويبنون قصورا فتصبح قصورهم قبورا وجمعهم بورا وسعيهم هباء منثورا ودعاؤهم ثبورا هذه صفتها وكان أمر الله قدرا مقدورا والصلاة والسلام على محمد عبده ورسوله المرسل إلى العالمين بشيرا ونذيرا وسراجا منيرا وعلى من كان من أهله وأصحابه له في الدين ظهيرا وعلى الظالمين نصيرا وسلم تسليما كثيرا أما بعد فإن الدنيا عدوة لله وعدوة لأولياء الله وعدوة لأعداء الله أما عداوتها لله فإنها قطعت الطريق على عباد الله ولذلك
10:24.english: Praise be to God, who made His friends acquainted with the calamitous snares of this world and its afflictions, and uncovered for them its defects and its shameful parts, until they gazed upon its evidences and its signs, and weighed its evil deeds against its good deeds. Thus they came to know that its objectionable aspects exceed its commendable ones, that what is hoped from it does not fulfill what is feared from it, and that its rising is not safe from its eclipse. Yet it is in the likeness of a comely woman who draws people to herself by her beauty — while within her are hidden secrets of evil, ugly things that destroy those who yearn for union with her. Then she is a fleer from her seekers, niggardly in her turning toward them; and when she does turn, one is not secure from her evil and her pestilence. If she does good for an hour, she does evil for a year; and if she does evil once, she makes it her perpetual habit. So the cycles of her turning are ever more tightly drawn, and the commerce of her sons is losing and ruined, and her afflictions in succession strike the breasts of her seekers, and the courses of her states proclaim the humiliation of those who pursue her. Thus every one deluded by her is destined to abasement, and every one who waxes proud through her proceeds to regret. Her very nature is to flee from her seeker and to be sought by the one who flees from her. Whoever serves her, she eludes; whoever turns away from her, she comes to. Her clarity is never free of the admixture of turbidity, nor is her joy ever disentangled from what embitters it. Her soundness bequeaths sickness, her youth drives on to decrepitude, and her bliss bears no fruit but remorse and regret. She is deceitful, guileful, fleeting, evasive. She never ceases adorning herself for her seekers until, when they have become her lovers, she bares her fangs at them, disorders the ordered strands of their affairs, and uncovers for them the hidden store of her wonders — then she makes them taste the lethal poisons and strikes them with the piercing shafts of her arrows. While her companions are in joy and bounty from her, suddenly she turns away from them as though she were but scattered dreams; then she rushes upon them with her calamities, grinds them as grain is ground, and shrouds them in their winding-sheets beneath the dust. If she has possessed one of them with all that the sun has risen upon, she makes him as reaped harvest, as though he had not dwelt in plenty the day before. Her companions desire joy from her, and she promises them delusion — until they hope for much and build palaces, and then their palaces become graves, their gatherings become ruin, their striving becomes scattered dust, and their cry becomes "Woe and destruction!" Such is her description — and the command of God is a decree determined. And the prayer and peace be upon Muhammad, His servant and His Messenger, sent to the worlds as a bringer of glad tidings and a warner, and as an illuminating lamp; and upon those of his family and companions who were for him supporters in the religion, and against the wrongdoers helpers; and abundant peace.
10:24.section_title_en: The Book of Condemnation of This World — Being the Sixth Book of the Quarter of the Destructive Things from The Revival of the Religious Sciences
10:24.anchors:
- Root: لهم (l-h-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core root meaning of swallowing, devouring, or ingesting wholly
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): الإلهام: casting something into the heart (al-rawʿ), specifically from God or the higher assembly; the root denotes the soul's complete reception, as one who swallows entirely
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: ألهمه الله الخير — God cast good into his heart. Metaphorical: جيش لهم — an army that engulfs and swallows whomever enters it
- Root: دنا (d-n-w)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Nearness in place, time, or rank; the world (al-dunyā) is so named because it is nearer and lower, deferred from the Hereafter
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): الدنو: proximity by essence or by judgment, used of place, time, and station; al-dunyā is the nearer, lower life
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: هو دانٍ — he is near. Metaphorical: الأدنى — the inferior, the baser, contrasted with what is better
- Root: حسر (ḥ-s-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Uncovering, stripping away a covering; exhaustion from exposure of one's strength
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): الحسر: uncovering what veils; al-ḥasīr: one whose strength is laid bare and spent; al-ḥāsir: the weary whose powers are uncovered as exhausted
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: حسر عن ذراعيه — he bared his forearms. Metaphorical: فلان كريم المحسر — so-and-so is noble when tested/examined (his hidden quality is uncovered)
- Root: سرر (s-r-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Concealment, the secret kept hidden in the breast; the innermost
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): الإسرار: opposite of declaration; al-sirr: the speech concealed in the soul
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: أسر الحديث — he concealed the speech. Metaphorical: أعطيتك سره — I gave you its choicest essence; هو في سر النسب — he is in the pure core of lineage
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The permissibility of interposing elements between a governing word and its governed prepositional phrase when the interposed element is complete in itself, as in the rhetorical suspensions of this oration
