10:24.arabic: ينقضي العمر حتى إذا أخذت الأرض زخرفها وازينت وظن أهلها أنهم قادرون عليها أتاها أمرنا ليلا أو نهارا فجعلناها حصيدا كأن لم تغن بالأمس فضرب الله تعالى لها مثلا فقال تعالى واضرب لهم مثل الحياة الدنيا كماء أنزلناه من السماء فاختلط به نبات الأرض فأصبح هشيما تذروه الرياح والزهد في الدنيا لما أن كان ملكا حاضرا حسده الشيطان عليه فصده عنه ومعنى الزهد أن يملك العبد شهوته وغضبه فينقادان لباعث الدين وإشارة الإيمان وهذا ملك بالاستحقاق إذ به يصير صاحبه حرا وباستيلاء الشهوة عليه يصير عبدا لفرجه وبطنه وسائر أغراضه فيكون مسخرا مثل البهيمة مملوكا يستجره زمام الشهوة آخذا بمختنقه إلى حيث يريد ويهوى ف
10:24.english: ...anxieties in [worldly] administrations, and likewise all the other means to rank. Then, whenever the means are secured and completed, the lifespan expires — until, when the earth has taken on its ornament and is adorned, and its people suppose that they are able to master it, there comes to it Our command by night or by day, and We make it a harvested stubble as if it had not flourished the day before. Thus God — exalted be He — struck for it a parable, saying — exalted be He: {And strike for them the parable of the life of this world: like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, and then it becomes dry chaff which the winds scatter} {«وَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلَ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا كَمَاءٍ أَنْزَلْنَاهُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَاخْتَلَطَ بِهِ نَبَاتُ الْأَرْضِ فَأَصْبَحَ هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ»} [Al-Kahf: 45]. And asceticism (al-zuhd) in this world — because it was a present sovereignty — Satan envied him for it and barred him from it.
10:24.section_title_en: On Renouncing Status and the True Meaning of Sovereignty — The Cure for the Love of Prestige
10:24.anchors:
- Root: ملك (malaka)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes possession, dominion, and the power to command and forbid; al-Farahidi notes its application to kingship and ownership alike.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Distinguishes two modes: (1) actual possession/sovereignty (al-tamalluk wa al-tawallī) and (2) the capacity/power to exercise it (al-quwwah ʿalā dhālika), whether or not one actually rules. True sovereignty belongs to him who governs his own soul.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (haqīqah): ownership of property and dominion over subjects. Metaphorical (majāz): "he mastered his anger" (malaka nafsahu ʿinda al-ghadab) — self-mastery as the paradigmatic figurative extension of kingship.
- Root: عقد (ʿabada)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Servitude and worship; the slave (ʿabd) is one who is owned and subjugated.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): ʿUbūdiyyah is the state of being subjugated to another's command; true slavery to passion is the degradation of the rational soul.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: chattel slavery. Metaphorical: he who is led by his lusts is a slave in reality, even if free in legal form.
- Root: سخر (sakhkhara)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To subjugate, compel, and employ against one's will; used of beasts and forces pressed into service.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Taskhīr is the compelled employment of a thing for another's purpose — the opposite of free, rational agency.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: subjugation of animals. Metaphorical: the man ruled by appetite is musakhkhar — driven like a beast by its halter.
- Root: دنا (dānā)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Nearness in place, time, or rank.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-dunyā (the lower world) is so named for its nearness and lowness relative to the Hereafter; it is the realm of delusion when pursued for its own sake.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: proximity. Metaphorical: the "nearer" life as the inferior, contemptible portion.
- Sibawayh Rule: Bāb al-faṣl bayna al-jār wa al-majrūr (Prepositional Interposition) — The periodic sentence structure here interposes lengthy causal and conditional clauses between the governing verb and its complements, requiring the translator to preserve the logical sequence of protasis and apodosis without collapsing the rhetorical tension of the original.
10:24.topic: Al-Ghazali on purifying the character, moral diseases, and spiritual remedies, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

10:24.arabic: على القرب وهو كما مثله الله تعالى حيث قال إنما مثل الحياة الدنيا كماء أنزلناه من السماء فاختلط به نبات الأرض الآية وقال تعالى واضرب لهم مثل الحياة الدنيا كماء أنزلناه من السماء إلى قوله فأصبح هشيما تذروه الرياح وكل ما تذروه رياح الموت فهو زهرة الحياة الدنيا وكل ما لا يقطعه الموت فهو الباقيات الصالحات فقد عرفت بهذا أن كمال القدرة بالمال والجاه كمال ظني لا أصل له وأن من قصر الوقت على طلبه وظنه مقصودا فهو جاهل وإليه أشار أبو الطيب بقوله ومن ينفق الساعات في جمع ماله .
10:24.english: Therefore, the perfections are three, if we count non-change through appetites and non-submission to them as a perfection—like the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of freedom. By "freedom" I mean non-enslavement to appetites and to willing worldly causes. The perfection of power for the servant is a path to acquiring the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of freedom, but he has no path to acquiring the perfection of power that endures after his death. For his power over the very substances of wealth and over subjugating hearts and bodies is cut off by death, whereas his knowledge and his freedom are not annihilated by death; rather, they both endure as perfection within him and as a means to nearness to God—may He be exalted.
10:24.section_title_en: On True Perfection: Knowledge and Freedom Over Power, Wealth, and Status
10:24.anchors:
- Root: قدر (q-d-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of measuring, determining, and enabling; power as capacity to bring about an effect.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): True power (qudrah) belongs absolutely to God alone; for humans, it is a relative capacity, never absolute, and is a means, not an end.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (haqiqah) power is God's; metaphorical (majaz) attribution of "power" to creatures is restricted and conditional, tied to specific acts.
- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Knowledge as apprehension of a thing's reality; also traces and signs by which one is guided.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Knowledge (ʿilm) is the apprehension of a thing's true nature or the judgment of existence or non-existence regarding it; it is the enduring perfection of the soul.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "he knew" as direct awareness; metaphorical: "he knew" as perception or discernment of signs (maʿālim) leading to truth.
- Root: موت (m-w-t)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Death as the cessation of vital functions; also the state of being inanimate or lifeless.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Death is the opposite of life; in theological context, it marks the termination of worldly capacities but not of the soul's acquired knowledge or freedom.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: physical death; metaphorical: "death" of the heart through ignorance or enslavement to passion, and "revival" of the land through rain as a similitude for the fleeting world.
- Sibawayh Rule: Restriction and Focused Predication (الحصر والتقييد بإنما) — Used to confine true perfection exclusively to knowledge and freedom, negating it for power, wealth, and status.
10:24.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Condemnation of Status and Ostentation'

11:11.arabic: على العمل فقال تعالى إلا الذين صبروا وعملوا الصالحات الحالة الثانية حالة العمل كي لا يغفل عن الله في أثناء عمله ولا يتكاسل عن تحقيق آدابه وسننه ويدوم على شرط الأدب إلى آخر العمل الأخير فيلازم الصبر عن دواعي الفتور إلى الفراغ وهذا أيضا من شدائد الصبر ولعله المراد بقوله تعالى نعم أجر العاملين الذين صبروا أي صبروا إلى تمام العمل الحالة الثالثة بعد الفراغ من العمل إذ يحتاج إلى الصبر عن إفشائه والتظاهر به للسمعة والرياء والصبر عن النظر إليه بعين العجب وعن كل ما يبطل عمله ويحبط أثره كما قال تعالى ولا ت
11:11.english: The first kind is obedience. The servant stands in need of patience in performing it, for patience in obedience is severe. This is because the soul (al-nafs) is by its very nature (bi-ṭabʿihā) averse to servitude (al-ʿubūdiyyah) and covets lordship (al-rubūbiyyah). For this reason, one of the knowers of God (al-ʿārifīn) said: "There is no soul but that it conceals within itself what Pharaoh displayed when he said, 'I am your lord most high' {أنا ربكم الأعلى} — but Pharaoh found for it a scope and an acceptance, so he manifested it when he vilified his people and they obeyed him. And there is no one but that he claims this [very thing] with respect to his slave, his servant, his followers, and every one who is under his subjugation and obedience — even if he refrains from manifesting it. For his fury and rage at their shortcomings in serving him, and his enslaving them [in that rage], issues only from an inner concealment of pride (al-kibr) and a contesting of lordship (munāzaʿat al-rubūbiyyah) within the mantle of majesty (ridāʾ al-kibriyāʾ)."
11:11.section_title_en: On Patience in Obedience and Abstinence from Disobedience — The Two Categories of Volitional Acts
11:11.anchors:
- Root: صبر (ṣ-b-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of restraint and retention under constraint; al-Farahidi notes its application to holding back.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الصبر: الإمساك في ضيق" — restraint within hardship; the soul's confinement to what reason and Law require, or its abstention from what they require it to abstain from. It is a generic term whose specific names vary by context: in tribulation it is patience (ṣabr) against despair (jazaʿ); in battle it is courage (shajāʿah) against cowardice.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "صبرت على ما أكره" (I bore patiently what I dislike) and "صبرت عما أحب" (I held back from what I love). Metaphorical (majāz): "صبرت يمينه" (I bound him by a stringent oath) — extended to any firm constraining.
- Root: ع م ل (ʿ-m-l)
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العمل: كل فعل يكون من الحيوان بقصد" — every purposeful act of a living being; more specific than mere "act" (fiʿl), and applies to both righteous and wicked deeds.
- Root: ن ف س (n-f-s)
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The soul (nafs) as the seat of volition and desire; its innate inclination (ṭabʿ) is central to Ghazali's argument here.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "نفس" as the self; metaphorical: "دفق نفسه" (he poured out his blood/life).
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction and Focused Predication with innamā) — governing the Prophet's dictum «إنما الأعمال بالنيات» where the predicate is restricted exclusively to intention.
11:11.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

11:38.arabic: عند اشتغاله بعمل السفينة قال {إن تسخروا منا فإنا نسخر منكم كما تسخرون} فهذا أحد النظرين النظر الثاني نظر من لم يبلغ إلى مقام الفناء عن نفسه وهؤلاء قسمان قسم لم يثبتوا إلا وجود أنفسهم وأنكروا أن يكون لهم رب يعبد وهؤلاء هم العميان المنكوسون وعماهم في كلتا العينين لأنهم نفوا ما هو الثابت تحقيقا وهو القيوم الذي هو قائم بنفسه وقائم على كل نفس بما كسبت وكل قائم فقائم به ولم يقتصروا على هذا حتى أثبتوا أنفسهم ولو عرفوا لعلموا أنهم من حيث هم هم لا ثبات لهم ولا وجود لهم وإنما وجودهم من حيث أوجدوا لا من حيث وجدوا وفرق بين الموج
11:38.english: From this station did Ḥabīb ibn Abī Ḥabīb look when he recited {«إِنَّا وَجَدْنَاهُ صَابِرًا نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ»} [We found him patient — an excellent servant, indeed he was oft-returning] and then exclaimed: "How astonishing! He gave and He praised!" — signaling that when He praises His own giving, He praises Himself; so He is the Praiser and He is the Praised. And from this station did the Shaykh Abū Saʿīd al-Muhayyanī look when {«يُحِبُّهُمْ وَيُحِبُّونَهُ»} [He loves them and they love Him] was recited before him, and he said: "By my life, He loves them — leave Him to love them! By His right, He loves them — for He only loves Himself." He signaled thereby that He is the Loving and He is the Beloved.
11:38.section_title_en: The Two Visions: The Eye of Pure Unity and the Eye of Those Veiled from Self-Annihilation
11:38.anchors:
- Root: نظر (naẓar)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of "sight, gazing, contemplation" — both physical vision and intellectual perception.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological nuance: naẓar as "deliberative reflection" (ta'ammul) leading to knowledge of the divine — the inward eye of the heart.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = ocular sight; Metaphorical (majāz) = intellectual insight and spiritual vision.
- Root: فنو (fanā')
  * Lisan / Ayn: Root meaning of "passing away, perishing, ceasing to be."
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological nuance: fanā' as the annihilation of the self's independent consideration — not physical extinction but the obliteration of the illusion of otherness beside God.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal = perishing of a thing; Metaphorical = the mystic's passing away from self-awareness into pure divine contemplation.
- Root: قوم (qawm)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of "standing, rising, being established."
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): al-Qayyūm (القيوم) — the Self-Subsisting One by whom all else stands; theologically distinct from al-Qā'im (the standing one).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal = physical standing; Metaphorical = self-subsistence and sustaining others.
- Sibawayh Rule: Rule of Restriction and Focused Predication (باب الحصر والتقييد) — governing the exclusive predication in "He is the Thankful and the Thanked" (هو الشاكر وهو المشكور), where the definite predicate restricts the attribution solely to God.
11:38.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

14:2.arabic: عن هذا الترجيح بالملك وهو مجاز محض إذ لا ملك إلا لملك الملوك الذي له ما في السموات والأرض وكيف يكون العبد مالكا وهو في نفسه ليس يملك نفسه بل هو ملك غيره نعم الخلق عباد الله والأرض مائدة الله وقد أذن لهم في الأكل من مائدته بقدر حاجتهم كالملك ينصب مائدة لعبيده فمن أخذ لقمة بيمينه واحتوت عليها براجمه فجاء عبد آخر وأراد انتزاعها
14:2.english: ...to your heart, so that your heart becomes bound by it, and thus your body becomes bound in that direction in a posture of stillness and solemnity when you worship your Lord. Likewise, your actions are divided into those that are noble — such as acts of obedience — and those that are base — such as relieving oneself or spitting. So when you spit toward the direction of the Qiblah, you have indeed wronged it (ẓalamtahā) and shown ingratitude for the blessing (niʿmah) of Allah Most High upon you, by virtue of His placing the Qiblah, through whose placement the perfection of your worship is achieved. Similarly, when you put on your leather sock (khuff) and begin with the left foot, you have wronged (ẓalamta), because the sock is a protection for the foot; the foot has a share in it, and in matters of shares and portions, one ought to begin with the nobler — that is justice (al-ʿadl) and fidelity to wisdom, while its opposite is injustice (ẓulm) and ingratitude for the blessing of the sock and the foot. And this, in the eyes of the knowers (al-ʿārifīn), is a grave offense (kabīrah), even if the jurist (al-faqīh) labels it merely "disliked" (makrūh) — to the extent that one of them (the righteous predecessors) had gathered many measures of wheat and was giving them in charity, and when asked about the reason, he said: "I once put on a sandal and began with the left foot inadvertently, so I wish to expiate that (kufr) through charity." Yes, the jurist is unable to magnify the matter in these affairs, because he is constrained — rather, he is occupied with reforming the common folk (al-ʿawāmm), whose rank approaches the rank of the beasts (al-anʿām), and they are plunged into darknesses (ẓulumāt) far greater and more immense than that such minor darknesses should appear in comparison to them. For it would be ugly to say of one who drank wine and took the cup with his left hand that he transgressed in two respects — one being the drinking, and the other the taking with the left — and of one who sold wine at the time of the call to prayer on Friday, it would be ugly to say he betrayed in two respects — {one} the selling of wine, and the other the selling at the time of the call. And of one who relieved himself in the prayer niche (miḥrāb) of a mosque with his back to the Qiblah, it would be ugly to mention his abandonment of propriety in relieving himself, in that he did not place the Qiblah to his right. For all sins are darknesses, some piled atop others, such that one is eclipsed beside another. A master may punish his slave if he uses his knife without his permission — but if he killed his most beloved son with that very knife, the unauthorized use of the knife would retain no weight or sting in itself. Thus, all the etiquettes (ādāb) that the Prophets and the Saints (al-awliyāʾ) observed, and which we have treated leniently in jurisprudence (fiqh) concerning the common folk, have as their cause this very necessity. Otherwise, all these disliked acts are deviations from justice (al-ʿadl), ingratitude for blessing (kufrān al-niʿmah), and a deficiency in the rank that conveys the servant to the degrees of proximity (darajāt al-qurb) — some of them affect the servant by diminishing proximity and lowering station, while others expel him entirely from the bounds of proximity into the realm of distance (ʿālam al-buʿd), which is the abode of the devils. Likewise, whoever breaks a branch from a tree without an urgent pressing need, and without a sound purpose, has shown ingratitude for the blessing of Allah Most High in the creation of trees and the creation of the hand. As for the hand, it was not created for frivolity, but for obedience and for deeds that aid in obedience. As for the tree, Allah Most High created it, and created for it roots, and conveyed water to it, and placed within it the power of nourishment and growth, so that it might reach the culmination of its development (munthā nashwihi), and His servants might benefit from it. So breaking it before its culmination, not in a manner by which His servants benefit, is a violation of the purpose of wisdom and a deviation from justice. But if he has a sound purpose, then that is permissible for him — for trees and animals have been made a ransom (fidāʾ) for the purposes of human beings, since both are perishable and doomed. Thus, annihilating the baser (al-akhass) for the preservation of the nobler (al-ashraf) for a time is closer to justice than squandering both. And to this points His saying, Most High: {«وَسَخَّرَ لَكُم مَّا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًا مِّنْهُ»} — "And He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth — all from Him" [Al-Jāthiyah: 13]. Yes — if he breaks a tree belonging to someone else, he is also a wrongdoer (ẓālim), even if he is in need, because every specific tree does not suffice for the needs of all the servants of Allah; rather, it suffices for a single need. And if one single person were to be singled out for it without preponderance (tarjīḥ) and specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), that would be injustice. So the one entitled to specification is he who obtained the seed, placed it in the ground, conveyed water to it, and undertook its care — he is more worthy of it than others, and his side is thereby established. But if it grew in dead land (mawāt al-arḍ) without any human effort, then one must seek another specification — namely, precedence in taking it (sabq ilā akhdhihi). For the one who precedes has the special property of precedence (khāṣṣiyyat al-sabq). Justice, then, is that he be most worthy of it. And the poor (al-fuqarāʾ) have expressed this preponderance by the term "ownership" (al-milk) — but it is pure metaphor (majāz maḥḍ), for there is no owner except the King of Kings (Malik al-Mulūk), to Whom belongs what is in the heavens and the earth. And how could a servant be an owner, when he himself does not own his own self — rather, he is the property of Another? Yes — the creatures are the servants of Allah, and the earth is the table (māʾidah) of Allah, and He has permitted them to eat from His table to the measure of their need — like a king who sets a table for his slaves. So if one takes a morsel with his right hand, and his fingers close over it, and another slave comes and seeks to snatch it away...
14:2.section_title_en: The Etiquette of the Heart and the Hidden Dimensions of Violating Sacred Directions and Blessings
14:2.anchors:
- Root: ظلم (ẓ-l-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is "darkness" (ẓulmah) — absence of light; also "to place something in other than its proper place" (waḍʿ al-shayʾ fī ghayr mawḍiʿihi).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Ẓulm is expressed via "darknesses" (ẓulumāt) as ignorance, polytheism, and transgression — the opposite of nūr (light/justice).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "الظلم ظلمات يوم القيامة" — injustice is darknesses on the Day of Judgment. Metaphorical (majāz): "أرض مظلومة" — land never dug, i.e., violated by first use; "ظلم البعير" — slaughtering an animal without cause (ʿabṭ).
- Root: نعم (n-ʿ-m)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Niʿmah is a state of well-being; also "softness" and "delicacy."
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Niʿmah is the good condition bestowed; its plural (niʿam) covers both little and much — "وَإِن تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا" {And if you count the blessings of Allah, you cannot enumerate them} [Ibrahim: 34].
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "جلت نعمة الله" — the blessing of Allah is immense. Metaphorical: "خفت نعامتهم" — their ostriches departed (i.e., they fled), showing how blessing can be "kicked away" (kufrān al-niʿmah).
- Root: ملك (m-l-k)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Ownership and dominion; the possessor (mālik) who disposes freely.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الملك: هو المتصرف بالأمر والنهي" — the king is one who commands and forbids; true ownership belongs only to Allah, "لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ" {To Him belongs what is in the heavens and the earth}.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "ملك يده" — what one's hand owns. Metaphorical: "ملكت فلانة أمرها" — she controlled her own affair; here, human "ownership" (milk) is pure metaphor (majāz maḥḍ), since real dominion is Allah's alone.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The rule governs how qualifying clauses (e.g., "التي بوضعها كمال عبادتك") attach to antecedents, preserving syntactic cohesion even when embedded phrases lengthen the sentence, ensuring no semantic break occurs between the act and its moral consequence.
14:2.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

14:12.arabic: واصبر على ما يقولون} وقال تعالى {ولنصبرن على ما آذيتمونا وعلى الله فليتوكل المتوكلون} وقال عز وجل {ودع أذاهم وتوكل على الله} وقال سبحانه تعالى فاصبر كما صبر أولي العزم من الرسل وقال تعالى {نعم أجر العاملين الذين صبروا وعلى ربهم يتوكلون} وهذا في أذى الناس وأما الصبر على أذى الحيات والسباع والعقارب فترك دفعها ليس من التوكل في شيء إذ لا فائدة فيه ولا يراد السعي ولا يترك السعي لعينه بل لإعانته على الدين وترتب الأسباب ههنا كترتبها في الكسب وجلب المنافع فلا نطول بالإعادة وكذلك في الأسباب الدافعة عن المال فلا ينقص التوكل بإغلاق باب البيت
14:12.english: ...and its end. Those who possess ends are called "the foremost" (al-sābiqūn), and those who possess beginnings are called "the companions of the right" (aṣḥāb al-yamīn). Then the companions of the right also have degrees, and likewise the foremost; and the highest degrees of the companions of the right adjoin the lowest degrees of the foremost. So there is no meaning to precise estimation in such matters. Rather, the verified truth is that tawakkul (reliance on God) through abandoning provision-storing (tark al-iddikhār) is not perfected except by the shortening of hope (qaṣr al-amal). As for the total absence of hopes for survival, its being stipulated is remote — even in a single soul — for that is as if impossible to exist. As for people, they vary in the length and shortness of hope. The least degree of hope is a day and a night, and what is less than that of hours; and its utmost is what can be conceived to be a man's lifespan. Between these are degrees beyond enumeration. Whoever does not hope for more than a month is closer to the goal than one who hopes for a year. And restricting it to forty [days] on account of the appointed time of Moses (peace be upon him) is far-fetched, for that incident was not intended to clarify the measure of what hope has been permitted. Rather, Moses' worthiness to attain the promised [encounter] was not completed except after forty days, due to a secret by which — and by its like — the sunnah of God most High proceeds in the gradual unfolding of matters, just as he (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed God kneaded the clay of Adam with His hand for forty mornings" {«إن الله خمر طينة آدم بيده أربعين صباحا»} — because the worthiness of that clay for kneading was dependent upon a period reaching what was mentioned. Therefore, whatever is beyond a year is not stored except by virtue of the heart's weakness and its leaning toward the outward aspects of causes; such [storing] falls outside the station of tawakkul, [the person] not being confident in the encompassing governance of the True Deputy (al-wakīl al-ḥaqq) over the hidden dimensions of causes. For the means of income — through harvests and alms — recur with the recurrence of years, generally speaking. Whoever stores for less than a year has a degree proportionate to the shortness of his hope; and whoever's hope is two months — his degree is not like the degree of one who hopes for a month, nor the degree of one who hopes for three months; rather, he is between them in rank. Nothing prevents storing except the shortness of hope. So the most virtuous is that one not store at all — even if his heart is weak — for the less his storing, the greater his merit. It has been related concerning the poor man whom the Prophet (peace be upon him) commanded ʿAlī (may God honor his face) and Usāmah to wash — so they washed him and shrouded him in his own cloak. When he buried him, he said to his companions: "He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with his face like the full moon on the night of the full moon; and were it not for one trait in him, he would be raised with his face like the radiant sun." We said: "And what is it, O Messenger of God?" He said: "He was a frequent faster, a frequent prayer-stancer, and abundant in the remembrance of God most High — except that when winter came, he stored the summer garment for his summer; and when summer came, he stored the winter garment for his winter." Then he (peace be upon him) said: "Rather, the least of what you have been given is certainty (al-yaqīn) and the resolve of patience (ʿazīmat al-ṣabr)" — the hadith. The jug and the knife and whatever is needed continuously — that is not the meaning of this; for storing such does not diminish the degree. As for the winter garment, it is not needed in summer. And this [censure] applies to one whose heart is not disturbed by abandoning storing, and whose soul does not look longingly toward the hands of creatures; rather, his heart turns to nothing except the True Deputy. But if he senses within himself a restlessness that occupies his heart away from worship, remembrance, and reflection, then storing is more appropriate for him. Indeed, even if he held onto an estate whose income sufficed for his needs, and his heart would not be free except through it, then that is more appropriate for him — because the goal is the rectification of the heart so that it may be emptied for the remembrance of God. There is a person whom the existence of wealth occupies, and a person whom its absence occupies; and what is harmful is whatever occupies one away from God (mighty and majestic). Otherwise, this world in itself is not harmful — neither its existence nor its absence. For this reason, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was sent to all classes of creation, among them merchants, craftsmen, and people of trades and industries. He did not command the merchant to abandon his trade, nor the craftsman to abandon his craft, nor did he command the one who had abandoned both to occupy himself with them. Rather, he called everyone to God most High and guided them to the fact that their triumph and salvation lie in the turning of their hearts away from this world toward God most High. The pillar of occupation with God (mighty and majestic) is the heart. So the correct course for the weak is to store the measure of his need, just as the correct course for the strong is to abandon storing.
14:12.section_title_en: On Reliance (Tawakkul): Degrees of Hope, Provision-Storing (Iddikhār), and the Means of Repelling Harm
14:12.anchors:
- Root: أمل (ʾ-m-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Prolonged expectation or hoping for something; the extension of one's aspiration toward a future state.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Hope (amal) is the soul's expectation of a beloved matter; its opposite is yaʾs (despair). In the Kalam context, it is tied to the length of one's expectation of worldly continuance, which directly governs the validity of tawakkul.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (haqīqah) usage denotes the temporal span of expectation; metaphorical (majāz) usage applies to the soul's attachment to causes. Here, Ghazali uses it literally to measure degrees of trust.
- Root: ذكر (dh-k-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To remember, to mention; the opposite of forgetfulness (nisyān).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Dhikr is the presence of the remembered thing in the heart; its highest form is absorption in the remembrance of God, which is the very purpose of heart-rectification (iṣlāḥ al-qalb).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: verbal mention; metaphorical: the heart's unwavering orientation toward the object of remembrance, as in "the heart's distraction from worship and dhikr."
- Root: سبب (s-b-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: A rope by which one climbs; a means or connection to something.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Everything by which one reaches something else is called a sabab. God has ordained causes (asbāb) as the customary channel (sunnah) of His decree; reliance is placed not on the cause itself but on the Causer of causes (musabbib al-asbāb).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a physical cord or link; metaphorical: any means, whether certain (maqṭūʿ), probable (maẓnūn), or illusory (mawhūm). Ghazali's tripartite division of causes rests on this rhetorical distinction.
- Root: وكل (w-k-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To entrust, to delegate; one who relies upon another as a deputy.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Tawakkul is to depend upon another and make him a deputy over one's affair. The true wakīl is God alone, for He alone encompasses the hidden dimensions of causes.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: delegation of authority; metaphorical: the heart's utter confidence in the deputy's sufficiency, as in "he entrusted his burden to God." Ghazali contrasts the strong (qawī) who abandons storing with the weak (ḍaʿīf) who stores out of necessity.
- Sibawayh Rule: Bāb al-ḥaṣr wa-l-taqyīd bi-innamā (Restriction and Focused Predication) — Used to delimit the conditions of tawakkul, e.g., "the one who stores is not excluded from tawakkul except by the length of his hope," and to distinguish what nullifies reliance from what does not.
14:12.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

14:12.arabic: إن كنتم مؤمنين وقال عز وجل وعلى الله فليتوكل المتوكلون وقال تعالى ومن يتوكل على الله فهو حسبه وقال سبحانه وتعالى إن الله يحب المتوكلين وأعظم بمقام موسوم بمحبة الله تعالى صاحبه ومضمون كفاية الله تعالى ملابسه فمن الله تعالى حسبه وكافيه ومحبه ومراعيه فقد فاز الفوز العظيم فإن المحبوب لا يعذب ولا يبعد ولا يحجب وقال تعالى أليس الله بكاف عبده فطالب الكفاية من غيره والتارك للتوكل هو المكذب لهذه الآية فإنه سؤال في معرض استنطاق بالحق كقوله تعالى هل أتى على الإنسان حين من الدهر لم يكن شيئا مذكورا وقال عز
14:12.english: Praise be to God, the Disposer of the dominion (mulk) and the spiritual sovereignty (malakūt), the One alone in majesty (ʿizzah) and omnipotence (jabarūt), Who raised the heaven without any pillar, and apportioned therein the provisions of His servants; Who turned the eyes of those possessed of hearts and intellects away from the observation of intermediaries and causes (al-wasāʾiṭ wa-l-asbāb) toward the Causer of causes (musabbib al-asbāb); and Who lifted their concern from turning toward anything other than Him, and from relying upon any disposer besides Him. Thus they worshipped none but Him alone — in knowledge that He is the One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge (al-ṣamad), the God — and in verification that all classes of creatures are servants like themselves, from whom no provision is sought, and that there is no atom but God created it, and no beast but upon God is its sustenance. When they verified that He is the Guarantor of His servants' provision and the Surety for it, they relied upon Him and said: {«حسبنا الله ونعم الوكيل»} — "God is sufficient for us, and what an excellent Guardian!" (Q. 3:173).
14:12.section_title_en: The Book of Divine Unity (Tawḥīd) and Reliance (Tawakkul) — Book Five of the Quarter of Deliverance from The Revival of the Religious Sciences
14:12.anchors:
- Root: وكل (w-k-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of delegating, entrusting, and appointing a deputy (wakīl) to manage one's affairs.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "التوكيل: أن تعتمد على غيرك وتجعله نائبا عنك" — Reliance (tawakkul) is the act of depending upon another and making him a deputy over your affair; its theological force is that God alone is the sufficient Guardian (wakīl), as in {«وكفى بالله وكيلا»}.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): appointing an agent; Metaphorical (majāz): the weak man who leans on others (وكل ووكلة تكلة). In the divine context, tawakkul is a real, not figurative, transfer of one's trust to God as the sole efficient cause.
- Root: سبب (s-b-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: A rope, cord, or means by which one ascends or reaches something; extended to any intermediary cause.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "سمي كل ما يتوصل به إلى شيء سببا" — Every means by which one reaches a goal is termed a cause (sabab); God is the "Musabbib al-Asbāb" (Causer of causes), transcending the causal ropes He suspends.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a physical cord; Metaphorical: any linkage or connection. Here, the "gaze upon causes" (mulāḥaẓat al-asbāb) is a metaphorical veiling of the true Agent.
- Root: حسب (ḥ-s-b)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To count, reckon, suffice; derived: ḥasb (sufficiency), ḥasīb (one who suffices, or the Reckoner).
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الحساب: استعمال العدد" — Counting; but in the divine attribute, "ḥasb" denotes God's all-sufficient guardianship, as in {«حسبنا الله ونعم الوكيل»}.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: reckoning by number; Metaphorical: "احتسبت ما عند فلان: اختبرته وسبرته" — to test and probe. God's being "Ḥasb" for the believer is a tested, verified sufficiency, not a mere claim.
- Root: غمض (gh-m-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To close the eye, to be obscure, low-lying, or hidden ground.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "يستعار للتغافل والتساهل" — closing the eye is metaphorically used for overlooking; here, the "ghumūḍ" (obscurity) of tawakkul is its conceptual hiddenness from the intellect.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a low, concealed place; Metaphorical: "أمر غامض" — a subtle, difficult affair. The text uses it for the doctrinal opacity of tawakkul.
- Sibawayh Rule: Interposition of the prepositional phrase (باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور) — The periodic structure "فلم يعبدوا إلا إياه" and "فقالوا حسبنا الله" shows the separation of the operative verb from its object for rhetorical emphasis, permissible where the pause is complete and the meaning remains unbroken.
14:12.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Monotheism and Reliance'

14:12.arabic: وإذا قال ولنصبرن على ما آذيتمونا فليكن حاله الصبر أو العزيمة عليه حتى يجد حلاوة التلاوة فإن لم يكن بهذه الصفات ولم يتردد قلبه بين هذه الحالات كان حظه من التلاوة حركة اللسان مع صريح اللعن على نفسه في قوله تعالى إلا لعنة الله على الظالمين وفي قوله تعالى كبر مقتا عند الله أن تقولوا ما لا تفعلون وفي قوله عز وجل وهم في غفلة معرضون وفي قوله فأعرض عمن تولى عن ذكرنا ولم يرد إلا الحياة الدنيا وفي قوله تعالى ومن لم يتب فأولئك هم الظالمون إلى غير ذلك من الآيات وكان داخلا في معنى قوله عز
14:12.english: And at the mention of God, His attributes, and His names, he bows low in humility before His majesty and in apprehension of His greatness. And at the mention of the disbelievers' sayings — those things impossible for God, Mighty and Majestic, such as their attributing to Him a son or a consort — he lowers his voice and inwardly recoils in shame at the ugliness of their speech. And at the description of Paradise, his innermost being surges forth with longing for it. And at the description of the Fire, his limbs tremble in fear of it. For when the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said to Ibn Mas'ud, "Recite to me," he said: "I began reciting Surah al-Nisa'. When I reached {فكيف إذا جئنا من كل أمة بشهيد وجئنا بك على هؤلاء شهيدا} [How then shall it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?] (4:41), I saw his two eyes overflowing with tears. He then said to me: 'That is enough for you now.'" And this was because the witnessing of that very state had wholly overwhelmed his heart.
14:12.section_title_en: The States of the Heart During Qur'anic Recitation — The Condition of the True Recieter
14:12.anchors:
- Root: وجل (w-j-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core root meaning of trembling fear, trepidation of the heart
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الوجل: استشعار الخوف" — the inward apprehension of fear; cited in {إنما المؤمنون الذين إذا ذكر الله وجلت قلوبهم}
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (Haqiqah): "رجل وجل، وقوم وجال" — a man fearful, a people fearful; the state of the heart's trembling before divine majesty
- Root: وصف (w-ṣ-f)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Describing a thing by its attributes and qualities
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الوصف: ذكر الشيء بحليته ونعته" — description is the mention of a thing by its adornment and attribute; may be true or false
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal vs Metaphorical: "وجهها يصف الحسن" — metaphorical usage where the face itself "describes" beauty; likewise, the tongue may "describe" falsehood, as in {ولا تقولوا لما تصف ألسنتكم الكذب}
- Root: وفي (w-f-y)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Completeness, fulfillment, reaching full measure
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الوافي: الذي بلغ التمام" — that which attains completion; "أوفى: إذا تمم العهد ولم ينقض حفظه" — fulfilled the covenant without breach
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "درهم واف" — a full-weight dirham; Metaphorical: "أوفى على المائة إذا زاد عليها" — surpassed the hundred
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The separation between the governing preposition and its object by intervening clauses, as in "فلما بلغت {فكيف إذا جئنا...}" where the temporal clause governs the narrative sequence
14:12.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Etiquette of Quran Recitation'

15:9.arabic: به فقد هدي ومن عمل به فقد فاز وقال تعالى {إنا نحن نزلنا الذكر وإنا له لحافظون} ومن أسباب حفظه في القلوب والمصاحف استدامة تلاوته والمواظبة على دراسته مع القيام بآدابه وشروطه والمحافظة على ما فيه من الأعمال الباطنة والآداب الظاهرة وذلك لا بد من بيانه وتفصيله وتنكشف مقاصده في أربعة أبواب الباب الأول في فضل القرآن وأهله الباب الثاني في آداب التلاوة في الظاهر الباب الثالث في الأعمال الباطنة عند التلاوة الباب الرابع في فهم القرآن وتفسيره بالرأي وغيره الباب الأول في فضل القرآن وأهله وذم المقصرين في تلاوته فضيلة القرآن
15:9.english: Praise be to God, who has bestowed His favor upon His servants through His sent Messenger (peace be upon him) and His revealed Book — falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation (tanzīl) from the Wise, the Praiseworthy {«تَنْزِيلٌ مِنْ حَكِيمٍ حَمِيدٍ»}. Through it, the path of reflection (iʿtibār) has been widened for the people of understanding, by virtue of what it contains of narratives and reports; and through it, the way of the upright course and the straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) has been made clear, by virtue of what it details of rulings and distinguishes between the lawful (ḥalāl) and the unlawful (ḥarām). It is the illumination and the light; through it is deliverance from delusion; in it is healing for what is in the breasts. Whoever opposes it among the tyrants, God crushes him; and whoever seeks knowledge in other than it, God leads him astray. It is the firm rope of God (ḥabl Allāh al-matīn), His manifest light, the trustworthy handhold (al-ʿurwah al-wuthqā), and the most faithful refuge. It encompasses the little and the much, the small and the great. Its wonders do not come to an end, nor do its marvels reach a limit. No delimitation (taḥdīd) encompasses its benefits according to the people of knowledge, nor does the frequency of repetition wear it out according to the people of recitation. It is that which guided the first and the last. When the jinn heard it, they did not delay in turning to their people as warners, saying: {«فَقَالُوا إِنَّا سَمِعْنَا قُرْآنًا عَجَبًا * يَهْدِي إِلَى الرُّشْدِ فَآمَنَّا بِهِ وَلَنْ نُشْرِكَ بِرَبِّنَا أَحَدًا»} ("Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Quran; it guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.") So whoever believes in it has been granted success (tawfīq); whoever speaks by it has spoken truthfully; whoever clings to it has been guided; and whoever acts by it has attained felicity (fawz). And God, the Exalted, says: {«إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ»} ("Indeed, We — it is We who have sent down the Remembrance, and indeed, We are its Preservers.") Among the means of its preservation (ḥifẓ) in hearts and in codices (maṣāḥif) is the constancy of its recitation (tilāwah) and perseverance in its study, along with the fulfillment of its etiquettes (ādāb) and conditions, and the safeguarding of what it contains of inward works (aʿmāl bāṭinah) and outward etiquettes (ādāb ẓāhirah). This cannot be done without its exposition and detailing; its aims unfold in four chapters (abwāb):
15:9.section_title_en: The Book of the Etiquettes of Quran Recitation — Section 220: The Excellence of the Quran and Its People
15:9.anchors:
- Root: نزل (n-z-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: "نزل: انحطاط من علو إلى سفل" — descent from a height to a lower place; the setting down of a thing in a place.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "النزول في الأصل هو انحطاط من علو... وإنزال الله تعالى نعمه ونقمه على الخلق، وإعطاؤهم إياها" — the descent of the Quran is a divine act of sending down (tanzīl) from the highest station, carrying with it the very mercy and address of God.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Haqiqah (literal): "نزل من علو إلى سفل" — physical descent. Majaz (metaphorical): "وأنزل الله الغيث، وأنزل الكتاب" — the "sending down" of revelation is a metaphorical extension denoting divine bestowal and elevation of the recipient, not spatial movement.
- Root: حفظ (ḥ-f-ẓ)
  * Lisan / Ayn: "الحفظ: الحِراسة والاستظهار" — guarding, preserving, and keeping watch over a thing.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الحفظ: ضبط الشيء عن أن يذهب أو يضيع" — the securing of a thing against loss or corruption; divine preservation (ḥifẓ) is an act of sovereign care.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Haqiqah: guarding a physical object. Majaz: "حفظ الله فلانًا" — divine protection from spiritual harm and error.
- Root: تلو (t-l-w)
  * Lisan / Ayn: "التلاوة: الاتباع، ثم سميت القراءة تلاوة لأنها تتبع الآيات حرفًا حرفًا" — following in sequence; recitation is so named because the reader follows the verses letter by letter.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "التلاوة: الإتيان بالشيء متتابعًا" — the bringing of a thing in succession; recitation of the Quran is the sequential utterance of its verses in devotion.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Haqiqah: following behind. Majaz: "تلا الكتاب" — reciting, as the tongue follows the written text.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The rule governing the separation of a preposition from its object by an intervening clause, as in «لا يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه ولا من خلفه», where the prepositional phrases are distributed across the sentence for rhetorical emphasis and comprehensiveness.
15:9.topic: Al-Ghazali's epistemic insights into the spiritual heart and inner faith, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

15:43.arabic: يترك الركون إلى الدنيا بقي في حزب الشيطان وإن جهنم لموعدهم أجمعين فإذا عرفت هذا تعجبت من قوم يقادون إلى الجنة بالسلاسل فما من أحد إلا وهو مقود الى الجنة بسلاسل الأسباب وهو تسليط العلم والخوف عليه وما من مخذول إلا وهو مقود إلى النار بالسلاسل وهو تسليط الغفلة والأمن والغرور عليه فالمتقون يساقون إلى الجنة قهرا والمجرمون يقادون إلى النار قهرا ولا قاهر إلا الله الواحد القهار
15:43.english: ...a beloved and an object of desire, or an abhorred and an object of aversion. And beyond the exposition of this subtle point lies the secret of Destiny (sirr al-qadar), the divulgence of which has been forbidden. And by this, the first difficulty is resolved—namely, how can gratitude be [required] when the grateful one has no share [in producing it]? And by this also the second is resolved: for by "gratitude" (shukr) we mean nothing other than the turning of God's blessing toward the direction of love for God. So when the blessing turns toward the direction of love—by God's act—then the intended purpose has been achieved. And your act is a gift from God, may He be exalted; and insofar as you are its locus (maḥall), He has praised you—and His praise is another blessing from Him to you. So it is He who gave, and it is He who praised; and one of His two acts became a cause (sabab) for the turning of His second act toward the direction of His love. To Him, therefore, belongs gratitude in every case; and you are described as "grateful" (shākir) only in the sense that you are the locus of that meaning which gratitude is an expression of—not in the sense that you are its efficient cause (mūjib). Just as you are described as "knowing" and "learned"—not in the sense that you create knowledge or bring it into existence, but in the sense that you are its locus, and it has come to be in you through the eternal power (al-qudrah al-azaliyyah). So your being described as "grateful" is an affirmation of thingness (shayʾiyyah) for you—and you are a thing, since He who made all things into things has made you a thing. Rather, you are a non-thing only when you suppose yourself to be a thing in your own essence. But with respect to the consideration of Him who made things into things, you are a thing, since He made you a thing. For if you cut off consideration of His making, you are a veritable non-thing. And to this the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, alluded when he said: "Act, for everyone is made facile for that for which he was created." {«حديث: اعملوا فكل ميسر لما خلق له»} — a hadith related from ʿAlī and ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, when it was said to him: "O Messenger of God, of what use is action, if matters have already been finished beforehand?" So it became clear that creatures are the channels (majārī) of God's power and the loci of His acts—even though they themselves are also among His acts. But some of His acts are loci for others. And His saying {«اعملوا»} ("Act"), even though it issued upon the tongue of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is itself one of His acts; and it is a cause for the creatures' knowledge that action is beneficial. And their knowledge is an act of God, may He be exalted; and knowledge is a cause for the arousal of a resolute inclination (dāʿiyyah jāzimah) toward movement and obedience. And the arousal of the inclination is also among God's acts; and it is a cause for the movement of the limbs—which also are among God's acts. But some of His acts are causes for others—that is, the first is a condition (sharṭ) for the second. Just as the creation of the body is a cause for the creation of the accident (ʿaraḍ), since the accident is not created before it; and the creation of life is a condition for the creation of knowledge; and the creation of knowledge is a condition for the creation of will (irādah). And all of it is from God's acts, some of them being causes for others—that is, conditions. And the meaning of its being a "condition" is that nothing is disposed to receive the act of life except a substance (jawhar); and nothing is disposed to receive knowledge except one possessed of life; and nothing is disposed to receive will except one possessed of knowledge. Thus, some of His acts are causes for others in this sense—not in the sense that some of His acts bring others into existence, but rather that they prepare and pave the way as conditions for the attainment of others. And this, when verified, ascends to the degree of divine unity (tawḥīd) which we have mentioned.
15:43.section_title_en: The Unveiling of the Secret of Destiny and the True Meaning of Gratitude and Action
15:43.anchors:
- Root: سبب (sababa)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The rope by which one climbs a palm tree; extended to any means by which one reaches a thing.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Every means (wasīlah) by which one arrives at something is called a sabab; God's "causing" (tasbīb) is the ordered chain of conditions and prerequisites.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (haqīqah): a physical cord or tie; Metaphorical (majāz): any causal connection, whether ontological or epistemic.
- Root: شكر (shakara)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To be full (of a well); to acknowledge and display a benefit.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "Shukr is the perception of the blessing and its manifestation." It is the heart's fullness with remembrance of the Benefactor, the tongue's praise, and the limbs' recompense.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: verbal thanks; Metaphorical: a beast that thrives on little fodder—i.e., the creature becomes a "locus" (maḥall) for the divine act.
- Root: خلق (khalaqa)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To measure, estimate, and create in due proportion.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "Creation is origination (ibdāʿ) from no prior model," and also "bringing forth one thing from another" (ījād al-shayʾ min al-shayʾ).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: the tailor's cutting and measuring; Metaphorical: God's bringing things into being upon a measure dictated by wisdom.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction & Focused Predication) — The restriction of attribution to a single agent (God) while preserving secondary causal descriptions for creatures as mere loci (maḥall) of divine acts.
15:43.topic: Al-Ghazali on purifying the character, moral diseases, and spiritual remedies, from 'Patience and Gratitude'

15:97.arabic: {واصبر على ما يقولون واهجرهم هجرا جميلا} وقال تعالى {ولقد نعلم أنك يضيق صدرك بما يقولون فسبح بحمد ربك} الآية وقال تعالى {ولتسمعن من الذين أوتوا الكتاب من قبلكم ومن الذين أشركوا أذى كثيرا وإن تصبروا وتتقوا فإن ذلك من عزم الأمور} أي تصبروا عن المكافأة ولذلك مدح الله تعالى العافين عن حقوقهم في القصاص وغيره فقال تعالى {وإن عاقبتم فعاقبوا بمثل ما عوقبتم به ولئن صبرتم لهو} خير الصابرين {وقال} صلى الله عليه وسلم صل من قطعك وأعط من حرمك واعف عمن ظلمك // ورأيت في الإنجيل قال عيسى بن مريم عليه السلام لقد قيل لكم من قبل إن السن بالسن والأنف بالأنف وأنا أقول
15:97.english: And acts of disobedience are the requisite of the impulse of caprice (bāʿith al-hawā). And the most severe kind of patience is patience in abstaining from those acts of disobedience that have become familiar through habit — for habit is a fifth nature. When habit is joined to lustful desire, two battalions from the battalions of Satan array themselves in concert against the battalion of God (jund Allāh) — may He be exalted — and the impulse of religion (bāʿith al-dīn) has no strength to suppress them. Then, if that act be one whose commission has been rendered easy (tayassara), patience in abstaining from it is heavier upon the soul — such as patience in abstaining from the sins of the tongue: backbiting (ghībah), falsehood, contentious disputation (mirāʾ), self-praise whether by insinuation (taʿrīḍ) or by explicit statement (taṣrīḥ), the varieties of jesting that wound hearts, the kinds of words by which one intends belittlement and contempt, and the mention of the dead with aspersion cast upon them, upon their sciences, their conduct, and their stations. For such mention is in its outward aspect (fī ẓāhirihi) backbiting, and in its inward aspect (fī bāṭinihi) self-praise. In it the soul has two lusts: one is the negation of the other [person], and the other is the affirmation of oneself. And by these two together there is completed for it that lordship (rubūbiyyah) which is innate in its disposition — and which is the very opposite of what it has been commanded regarding servanthood (ʿubūdiyyah). And because of the conjunction of the two lusts, and the ease of moving the tongue, and the fact that this becomes habitual in everyday converse, patience in abstaining from it becomes difficult. And it is among the greatest of the destructive enormities (al-mūbiqāt) — so much so that its disapproval and ugliness have been effaced from hearts by dint of its frequent repetition and the universality of familiarity with it. Thus you see a man who would, for example, wear silk and deem it utterly remote [of permissibility], yet he unleashes his tongue the whole day long against the reputations (aʿrāḍ) of people and does not deem that objectionable — notwithstanding what has come down in the report that backbiting is more severe than adultery (zinā). And God — may He be exalted — said: {«ودع أذاهم وتوكل على الله»} "And leave aside their harm and put thy trust in God" (Q. 33:48). And He said — may He be exalted: {«واصبر على ما يقولون واهجرهم هجرا جميلا»} "And be patient over what they say, and depart from them with a gracious departure" (Q. 73:10). And He said — may He be exalted: {«ولقد نعلم أنك يضيق صدرك بما يقولون فسبح بحمد ربك»} "And indeed We know that thy breast is straitened by what they say; so glorify with the praise of thy Lord" (Q. 15:97–98) — to the end of the verse. And He said — may He be exalted: {«ولتسمعن من الذين أوتوا الكتاب من قبلكم ومن الذين أشركوا أذى كثيرا وإن تصبروا وتتقوا فإن ذلك من عزم الأمور»} "And you shall surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate [others with God] much harm. And if you are patient and God-fearing, indeed that is of the resolute affairs" (Q. 3:186) — that is, that you be patient in refraining from requital (mukāfaʾah). And for this reason God — may He be exalted — praised those who pardon others their due rights in retaliation (qiṣāṣ) and otherwise, saying — may He be exalted: {«وإن عاقبتم فعاقبوا بمثل ما عوقبتم به ولئن صبرتم لهو خير الصابرين»} "And if you punish, then punish with the like of that wherewith you were afflicted. And if you are patient, it is surely better for the patient" (Q. 16:126). And he — upon him be peace — said: "Maintain the bond with him who cuts you off, and give to him who withholds from you, and pardon him who wrongs you." And I have seen in the Gospel that ʿĪsā ibn Maryam — upon him be peace — said: "It was said to you of old: an eye for an eye and a nose for a nose. But I say to you: do not resist evil. Rather, whoever strikes your right cheek, turn to him PageV04P071 the left cheek; and whoever takes your cloak, give him your garment; and whoever compels you to walk with him one mile, walk with him two miles." And all of that is a command to be patient under harm. So patience under the harm of people is among the highest stations of patience, because in it the impulse of religion and the impulse of lustful desire and anger are all arrayed together [against the soul].
15:97.section_title_en: The Most Severe Forms of Patience: Abstaining from Habitual Sins and Enduring Harm
15:97.anchors:
- Root: صبر (ṣ-b-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of restraint and withholding; "ṣabara al-dābbah" = to hold back an animal without fodder; "ṣabartu nafsī" = I restrained my soul.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الصبر: حبس النفس على ما يقتضيه العقل والشرع، أو عما يقتضيان حبسها عنه" — Patience is the withholding of the soul upon what reason and Law require, or from what they require it to be withheld. When exercised against calamity it is called ṣabr alone (opposed to jazaʿ); in warfare, courage (shajāʿah); in vexing misfortune, forbearance.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "صبرت على ما أكره. وصبرت عما أحب" — I bore patiently what I dislike, and I restrained myself from what I love. Metaphorical (majāz): "هو أصبر على الضرب من الأرض" — he is more enduring of beating than the earth.
- Root: عادة (ʿ-w-d)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Recurrence and return; habitual practice that becomes second nature through repetition.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Habit (ʿādah) as reiterated action that imprints upon the soul, rendering the act facile and its abandonment burdensome.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: return to a state or place. Metaphorical: the ingrained disposition that governs conduct.
- Root: غيب (gh-y-b)
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الغيب: مصدر غابت الشمس وغيرها: إذا استترت عن العين" — that which is concealed from the senses; applied to what is absent from human perception, though nothing is absent from God.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "تكلم بذلك عن ظهر الغيب" — he spoke of that behind the veil of the unseen. Metaphorical: "أتونا في غابة" — they came in a dense host (like tangled thickets).
- Sibawayh Rule: Prepositional Interposition (باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور) — governing the permissible separation between the preposition and its object for rhetorical emphasis, as in the periodic construction "فإن ذلك في ظاهره غيبة وفي باطنه ثناء على النفس" where the circumstantial qualifiers (ẓāhir/bāṭin) are interposed to contrast outward form with inward reality.

16:18.arabic: الأرض وآخرهم الخباز وإن تعدوا نعمة الله لا تحصوها // حديث لا يستدير الرغيف ويوضع بين يديك حتى يعمل فيه ثلثمائة وستون صانعا أولهم ميكائيل الحديث لم أجد له أصل وقال بعضهم أتيت قاسما الجرعي فسألت عن الزهد أي شيء هو فقال أي شيء سمعت فيه فعددت أقوالا فسكت فقلت أي شيء تقول أنت فقال اعلم أن البطن دنيا العبد فبقدر ما يملك من بطنه يملك من الزهد وبقدر ما يملكه بطنه تملكه الدنيا وكان بشر بن الحرث قد اعتل مرة فأتى عبد الرحمن الطبيب يسأله عن شيء يوافقه من المأكولات فقال تسألني فإذا وصفت لك لم تقبل مني قال صف
16:18.english: I left it upon a loaf of bread, then I met a boy and said: "Are you not the son of so-and-so, whose father has died?" He replied: "Yes." So I handed it to him. They said: And he came forward weeping and reciting: {«وَيُطْعِمُونَ الطَّعَامَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا»} — "And they give food, despite their love for it, to the poor, the orphan, and the captive" {«الإنسان: 8»}. Then he did not taste it after that, and he remained craving dates for years. Then one day, he bought dates for a qīrāṭ and raised them until nightfall to break his fast upon them. He said: Then a violent wind blew until the world grew dark, and the people were terrified. So ʿUtbah turned upon his self, saying: "This is for my audacity against You, and my buying of dates for a qīrāṭ." Then he said to his self: "I do not think that the people were seized except by your sin—on condition that you do not taste them." And Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī bought greens for half a fals and vinegar for a fals, and he spent his entire night saying to his self: "Woe to you, O Dāwūd! How long is your reckoning on the Day of Resurrection!" Then after that, he ate nothing but dry bread. And ʿUtbah al-Ghulām said one day to ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Zayd: "So-and-so describes of himself a station that I do not recognize in myself." He said: "Because you eat dates with your bread, while he adds nothing to his bread." He said: "If I abandon eating dates, will I recognize that station?" He said: "Yes, and others besides it." So he began to weep, and one of his companions said to him: "May Allah not make your eye weep—do you weep over dates?" ʿAbd al-Wāḥid said: "Leave him, for his self has recognized the sincerity of his resolve in abandonment, and when he abandons a thing, he does not return to it." And Jaʿfar ibn Naṣr said: Al-Junayd ordered me to buy for him the Wazīrī figs. When I bought them, he took one at the time of breaking the fast and placed it in his mouth, then he threw it out and began to weep. Then he said: "Carry it away." I said to him concerning that: "Why?" He said: "A caller called out to me: 'Are you not ashamed? You abandoned it for My sake, then you return to it?'" And Ṣāliḥ al-Murrī said: I said to ʿAṭāʾ al-Sulamī: "I am going to trouble myself for your sake with something, so do not reject my kindness." He said: "Do what you wish." He said: So I sent to him, with my son, a drink of sawīq which I had kneaded with butter and honey, and I said: "Do not leave until he drinks it." When the next day came, I prepared for him something similar, and he returned it and did not drink it. So I reproached him and blamed him for that, and I said: "Glory be to Allah! You have rejected my kindness." When he saw my distress over that, he said: "Do not let this grieve you. I did drink it the first time, and I tempted my self the second time to drink it, but I could not do so—whenever I wanted that, I remembered the saying of Allah the Exalted: {«يَتَجَرَّعُهُ وَلَا يَكَادُ يُسِيغُهُ»} — 'He will gulp it but will hardly swallow it' {«إبراهيم: 17»}." Ṣāliḥ said: So I wept and said to myself: "I am in one valley, and you are in another valley." And al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī said: "My self has been demanding of me for thirty years that I dip a carrot in molasses, and I have not fed it that." And Abū Bakr al-Jallāʾ said: "I know a man whose self says to him: 'I will be patient for you through ten days of hunger, then feed me after that a craving I desire.' He says to her: 'I do not want you to endure ten days of hunger, but abandon this craving.'" And it is related that a worshiper invited some of his brothers, and he placed before him loaves of bread. His brother began turning over the loaves to choose the finest among them, so the worshiper said to him: "Stop! What are you doing? Do you not know that in the loaf you have turned away from there is such-and-such wisdom, and such-and-such a maker worked upon it—until it was rounded from the cloud that carries the water, and the water that irrigates the earth, and the winds, and the earth, and the beasts, and the sons of Adam—until it reached you? Then after all this, you turn it over and are not satisfied with it?" And in the report: "A loaf is not rounded and placed before you until three hundred and sixty makers have worked upon it—the first of them is Michael (Mīkāʾīl), peace be upon him, who measures out the water from the treasuries of mercy, then the angels that drive the clouds, and the sun, and the moon, and the spheres, and the angels of the air, and the beasts of the earth, and the last of them is the baker. {«وَإِن تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا»} — 'And if you should count the favors of Allah, you could not enumerate them' {«إبراهيم: 34»}." — A hadith: "A loaf is not rounded and placed before you until three hundred and sixty makers have worked upon it—the first of them is Michael." — I have not found any basis for this hadith. And some of them said: I came to Qāsim al-Jurʿī and asked about asceticism (al-zuhd)—what it is. He said: "What have you heard about it?" So I enumerated various sayings, and he fell silent. Then I said: "What do you yourself say?" He said: "Know that the belly is the world (dunyā) of the servant. To the extent that he masters his belly, he masters of asceticism; and to the extent that his belly masters him, the world masters him." And Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith was once ill, so he came to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān the physician, asking him about something that would suit him among foods. He said: "You ask me, and when I describe something for you, you will not accept it from me." He said: "Describe it so that I may hear." He said: "Drink oxymel (sikanjabīn), suck on quince, and eat..."
16:18.section_title_en: The Revival of the Religious Sciences — Book on Trust (Tawakkul), Section 646: Ascetic Restraint in Food and the Discipline of the Self
16:18.anchors:
- Root: نفس (n-f-s)
  * Lisan / Ayn: The self, soul, or spirit; that which animates and carries the essential identity of a person.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): In theological usage, النفس denotes the inner reality of a person—whether the rational soul or the lower appetitive self (al-nafs al-ammārah)—which must be disciplined and opposed in its cravings.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) refers to the soul/self as the seat of volition; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to the "blood of life" (نفس سائلة), indicating that which, when spilled, renders impurity—here, the self is that which must be "broken" of its desires.
- Root: اكل (a-k-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To eat, consume, or take nourishment; the act of ingesting food.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): الأكل is the taking of food; metaphorically extended to fire consuming wood (أكلت النار الحطب). In ascetic contexts, it signifies the permissible boundary of bodily sustenance versus the indulgence of appetite.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: eating for survival. Metaphorical: "He ate my wealth" (أكل مالي) meaning he squandered it; here, the narratives pivot on the literal act of eating as the arena where the self's discipline is tested—whether one eats for need or for pleasure.
- Root: قال (q-w-l)
  * Lisan / Ayn: To say, speak, or utter; a statement or discourse.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): In Quranic and theological contexts, القول is not mere speech but the articulation of conviction or resolve—often used to contrast outward claims with inward reality.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: verbal utterance. Metaphorical: the "speech" of the self (حديث النفس) as internal dialogue, where the lower self addresses a person and must be answered with resolve.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The rule governing the separation of a preposition from its governed noun by an intervening clause, as seen in complex periodic sentences where the narrative flow is interrupted by parenthetical exhortations or Quranic citations, requiring precise parsing to maintain grammatical coherence.

16:90.arabic: والإحسان وإيتاء ذي القربى وينهى عن الفحشاء والمنكر والبغي وأنا رأيت منكرا فغيرته فقال فغيره فوالله ما قال إلا هذا فلما خرج أعطى الخليفة رجلا بدرة وقال اتبع الشيخ فإن رأيته يقول قلت لأمير المؤمنين وقال لي فلا تعطه شيئا وإن رأيته لا يكلم أحدا فأعطه البدرة فلما خرج من القصر إذا هو بنواة في الأرض قد غاصت فجعل يعالجها ولم يكلم أحدا فقال له يقول لك أمير المؤمنين خذه هذه البدرة فقال قل لأمير المؤمنين يردها من حيث أخذها ويروى أنه أقبل بعد فراغه من كلامه على النواة التي يعالج قلعها من الأرض وهو يقول أ
16:90.english: And it is astonishing that the Rāfiḍah went beyond this and said: "It is not permissible to enjoin the good as long as the infallible Imam — who, in their view, is the true Imam — has not come forth." These are too base in rank to be addressed; rather, their answer is to say to them: When they come to a judge seeking their rights concerning their blood and their wealth, [one says to them:] "If I aided you, that would be enjoining the good, and extracting your rights from the hands of those who wronged you would be forbidding the munkar — and your seeking your right is part of the good. But this is not the time for forbidding injustice and seeking rights, because the true Imam has not yet come forth."
16:90.section_title_en: The Fourth Condition: Authorization from the Imam and Governor — Its Invalidity, and the Five Ranks of Ḥisbah
16:90.anchors:
- Root: أ ذ ن (ʾ-dh-n)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is "permission" or "license" — to grant leave for an act; also "ear" (udhun), the instrument of hearing command.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): In theological usage, ʾidhn denotes divine or authoritative sanction that legitimizes an action; its absence renders the act transgressive (muʿtadā).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is "to permit"; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to the Imam's delegation of authority, which is a contingent, not essential, condition.
- Root: ن ك ر (n-k-r)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Nakirah denotes the unrecognized or the objectionable; munkar is that which the sound intellect and divine law repudiate.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Inkār is the heart's rejection of what it does not conceive as right; it opposes maʿrifah (recognition). The tongue's inkār may be true or feigned.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Nakira is stronger than ankara — the former is the heart's denial, the latter the eye's; here, munkar is the objective evil that the enjoiner must repel.
- Root: ع ر ف (ʿ-r-f)
  * Lisan / Ayn: ʿArafa means to know by trace or sign; maʿrūf is that which is well-known and approved by revelation and custom.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Maʿrifah is knowledge attained through reflection on effects — more specific than ʿilm; hence, al-amr bi-l-maʿrūf is commanding what is recognized as good by divine attestation.
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal sense is "to know"; here, maʿrūf is the established good, and its enjoining is a communal obligation independent of temporal authorization.
- Sibawayh Rule: Bāb al-ḥaṣr wa-l-taqyīd bi-innamā (Restriction and Specification) — The conditional clause "sharaṭa hādhā al-sharṭ" is a restrictive predication that the author refutes by universalizing the command (ʿalā al-ʿumūm), a syntactic move that nullifies the exception.

16:90.arabic: علي القرآن فقرأ عليه إن الله يأمر بالعدل والإحسان وإيتاء ذي القربى الآية فقال له فأعاد فقال والله إن له لحلاوة وإن عليه لطلاوة وإن أسفله لمورق وإن أعلاه لمثمر وما يقول هذا بشر (1) وقال الحسن والله ما دون القرآن من غنى ولا بعده من فاقة وقال الفضيل من قرأ خاتمة سورة الحشر حين يصبح ثم مات من يومه ختم له بطابع الشهداء ومن قرأها حين يمسي ثم مات من ليلته ختم له بطابع الشهداء وقال القاسم بن عبد الرحمن قلت لبعض النساك ما ههنا أحد نستأنس به فمد يده إلى المصحف ووضعه على حجره وقال هذا وقال علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه ث
16:90.english: God, may He be exalted, said: {«...»} (1)
16:90.section_title_en: The Virtues of the Qur'an — Section 221: Hadiths and Reports on the Excellence of Qur'anic Recitation
16:90.anchors:
- Root: قرا (Qara'a)
  * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of reading/reciting; Al-Khalil notes the root's connection to gathering and collecting letters into articulated speech.
  * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological nuance — recitation (tilāwah) as the act of following the Qur'an's words with attentive devotion; the term qāri' extends to one who is a devoted worshipper (nāsik).
  * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal vs Metaphorical — literally "reading/reciting"; metaphorically applied to the one who devotes himself to worship through recitation, as in Jarīr's verse.
- Sibawayh Rule: Prepositional Interposition (al-faṣl bayn al-jār wa-al-majrūr) — governing the syntactic placement of qualifying phrases within hadith citations.
